The Hershey Company
CALIFORNIA TRANSPARENCY IN SUPPLY CHAINS ACT

The Hershey Company, together with its subsidiaries, recognizes the importance of the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010, which is designed to increase the amount of information manufacturers and retailers make available regarding their efforts to address issues related to slavery and human trafficking in their supply chains. We endeavor to model good business practices by striving to ensure our supply chains are responsibly managed.

Hershey has a history of operating with high ethical standards and integrity. The manner in which our employees and vendors manage social, environmental, and economic impacts is critical to our long-term business success.

We have established a Supplier Code of Conduct that sets forth Hershey’s standards and expectations for suppliers with respect to corporate and social responsibility. We require our suppliers to acknowledge their understanding of and adhere to our Supplier Code of Conduct, which serves as a key governing component of our business relationship with these third parties.

As outlined in the Supplier Code of Conduct, our goal is to work with our suppliers to assure compliance with the following requirements:

Legal and Compliance

Suppliers must comply with all applicable laws and regulations in their country of operation.

Social and Working Conditions

Forced Labor: Suppliers must not utilize or benefit in any way from forced or compulsory labor nor utilize factories or subcontractors that force unpaid labor.

Child Labor: Hershey is committed to the elimination from its supply chain of the worst forms of child labor, as defined by the International Labor Organization (ILO) Convention 138 and 182. We expect our suppliers to support and participate in industry efforts aimed at the elimination of such practices, wherever they exist in the supply chain.

Working Hours and Wages: Suppliers should provide wages at least equal to the applicable legal minimum wage and any associated statutory benefits, and working hours should reflect applicable legal norms, which includes supplier compliance with applicable laws regarding working and overtime hours.

Freedom of Association: Consistent with local regulations, employees’ right to freedom of association should be respected by suppliers, including that employee relationships are voluntary in nature.

Non-Discrimination: Supplier hiring and employment decisions should be made solely on the basis of skill, ability and performance by the workers, and discrimination is not permitted on the basis of race, religion, gender, political opinion, national extraction, or social origin.

Health and Safety: Suppliers must provide employees with safe and health working environments and practices must comply with all relevant local and national laws, codes, and regulations.

Supplier Verification and Audits

Hershey reserves the right to monitor, review and verify supplier compliance with the principles set forth in the Supplier Code of Conduct, either through third-party certifications or a responsible sourcing audit, which may be performed by a third party. In the event the Company becomes aware of non-compliance, we maintain the right to set forth corrective actions and/or terminate our business relationship with the supplier.

Hershey requires key suppliers to undergo the Sedex Members Ethical Trade Audit (SMETA), developed by the Associate Auditor Group of the Sustainable Ethical Data Exchange. SMETA is a prescriptive audit procedure that is a compilation of effective ethical audit techniques.

In 2013, Hershey used third-party auditors to complete social assessments on 25 percent of its external suppliers (based on spend). In 2014, Hershey used third-party auditors to begin assessing an additional 25 percent of its external suppliers (based on spend).

Code of Ethical Business Conduct

Hershey has committed to operating with the highest of ethical standards. This commitment dates to the founding of our company and has earned Hershey a reputation for fairness and honesty throughout the world.

The Company’s Code of Ethical Business Conduct (Code of Conduct) sets forth the standards by which we conduct our operations and establishes a clear expectation that the standards be followed in all job-related activities, regardless of business pressure. It further memorializes our commitment to consumers by maintaining the trust consumers place in our brands, providing the best products in the market and adhering to honest marketing practices.

Employee Training

Our Code of Conduct is distributed to all Hershey employees and is supplemented by targeted training and communications addressing the values set forth within it. Every year employees must complete training modules or acknowledge the standards, guidelines and practices set for in our Code of Conduct. Non-compliance with the Code of Conduct and related Company policies may subject employees to discipline, up to and including termination.

The Hershey Company
CALIFORNIA TRANSPARENCY IN SUPPLY CHAINS ACT

The Hershey Company, together with its subsidiaries, recognizes the importance of the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010, which is designed to increase the amount of information manufacturers and retailers make available regarding their efforts to address issues related to slavery and human trafficking in their supply chains. We endeavor to model good business practices by striving to ensure our supply chains are responsibly managed.

Hershey has a history of operating with high ethical standards and integrity. The manner in which our employees and vendors manage social, environmental, and economic impacts is critical to our long-term business success.

We have established a Supplier Code of Conduct that sets forth Hershey’s standards and expectations for suppliers with respect to corporate and social responsibility. We require our suppliers to acknowledge their understanding of and adhere to our Supplier Code of Conduct, which serves as a key governing component of our business relationship with these third parties.

As outlined in the Supplier Code of Conduct, our goal is to work with our suppliers to assure compliance with the following requirements:

Legal and Compliance

Suppliers must comply with all applicable laws and regulations in their country of operation.

Social and Working Conditions

Forced Labor: Suppliers must not utilize or benefit in any way from forced or compulsory labor nor utilize factories or subcontractors that force unpaid labor.

Child Labor: Hershey is committed to the elimination from its supply chain of the worst forms of child labor, as defined by the International Labor Organization (ILO) Convention 138 and 182. We expect our suppliers to support and participate in industry efforts aimed at the elimination of such practices, wherever they exist in the supply chain.

Working Hours and Wages: Suppliers should provide wages at least equal to the applicable legal minimum wage and any associated statutory benefits, and working hours should reflect applicable legal norms, which includes supplier compliance with applicable laws regarding working and overtime hours.

Freedom of Association: Consistent with local regulations, employees’ right to freedom of association should be respected by suppliers, including that employee relationships are voluntary in nature.

Non-Discrimination: Supplier hiring and employment decisions should be made solely on the basis of skill, ability and performance by the workers, and discrimination is not permitted on the basis of race, religion, gender, political opinion, national extraction, or social origin.

Health and Safety: Suppliers must provide employees with safe and health working environments and practices must comply with all relevant local and national laws, codes, and regulations.

Supplier Verification and Audits

Hershey reserves the right to monitor, review and verify supplier compliance with the principles set forth in the Supplier Code of Conduct, either through third-party certifications or a responsible sourcing audit, which may be performed by a third party. In the event the Company becomes aware of non-compliance, we maintain the right to set forth corrective actions and/or terminate our business relationship with the supplier.

Hershey requires key suppliers to undergo the Sedex Members Ethical Trade Audit (SMETA), developed by the Associate Auditor Group of the Sustainable Ethical Data Exchange. SMETA is a prescriptive audit procedure that is a compilation of effective ethical audit techniques.

In 2013, Hershey used third-party auditors to complete social assessments on 25 percent of its external suppliers (based on spend). In 2014, Hershey used third-party auditors to begin assessing an additional 25 percent of its external suppliers (based on spend).

Code of Ethical Business Conduct

Hershey has committed to operating with the highest of ethical standards. This commitment dates to the founding of our company and has earned Hershey a reputation for fairness and honesty throughout the world.

The Company’s Code of Ethical Business Conduct (Code of Conduct) sets forth the standards by which we conduct our operations and establishes a clear expectation that the standards be followed in all job-related activities, regardless of business pressure. It further memorializes our commitment to consumers by maintaining the trust consumers place in our brands, providing the best products in the market and adhering to honest marketing practices.

Employee Training

Our Code of Conduct is distributed to all Hershey employees and is supplemented by targeted training and communications addressing the values set forth within it. Every year employees must complete training modules or acknowledge the standards, guidelines and practices set for in our Code of Conduct. Non-compliance with the Code of Conduct and related Company policies may subject employees to discipline, up to and including termination.

True Religion Apparel, Inc. Corporate Responsibility



True Religion Apparel, Inc., together with its subsidiaries and affiliates (collectively, the “Company”), is dedicated to upholding fair and legal employment practices and environmental sustainability requirements.

As an integral component of this commitment, we have developed and implemented an Associate Code of Conduct (the “Code,” available here), which applies to all vendors, manufacturers, contractors, and suppliers (“Associates”) that form a part of our supply chain.

The Code advises our Associates of their obligation to adhere to all applicable local, state (including the California Transparency in Supply Chain Act) and federal laws as well as the standards established by the Company and set forth in the Code.

The core elements of our Code are prohibitions on discrimination, forced labor, and child labor, insistence on fair wages and hours and the provision of safe and healthy working conditions, as well as guidelines for minimizing each Associate’s environmental footprint.

As a condition of doing business with the Company, each Associate must execute the Code and implement the principles contained therein.

The Company will continue to develop Associate monitoring systems including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced third party audits to assess and ensure compliance with the Code.

If the Company determines that any Associate has violated the Code, the Company may either terminate its business relationship or require the Associate to implement a corrective action plan.

By espousing the foregoing principles, the Company strives to ensure integrity of its supply chain while continuing to uphold and exceed the quality of our branded merchandise.



2012 California Transparency in Supply Chain Act (SB 657) (the “Act”)

The Act, which became effective January 1, 2012, requires certain retail sellers and manufacturers to disclose their efforts to eradicate slavery and human trafficking from their direct supply chains. It is intended to provide consumers with the means to determine which companies have an active social responsibility program and thereafter to make conscientious purchasing decisions.

The points outlined below highlight the Act’s mandatory disclosures, followed by an explanation of how the Company is addressing each of them:

(1) Verification

The Company continues to develop monitoring systems to assess and ensure Associate’s compliance with the slavery and human trafficking prohibitions set forth in the Code through various means, including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced on-site third party verification visits.

(2) Audits

The Company relies on independent third party vendors to conducts unannounced audits of Associates, which assist in the evaluation of Associates’ compliance with Company’s supply chain standards for trafficking and slavery.

(3) Integrity of Components

By executing the Code, every Associate certifies that materials incorporated into goods and merchandise manufactured for the Company comply with labor and trafficking laws, and with all other applicable laws, rules and regulations of the respective country or countries in which they do business.

(4) Accountability

Associates must manifest their commitment to the implementation of the Code’s stated anti-slavery and human trafficking principles by maintaining or establishing an appropriate management system (with adequate documentation and record-keeping in place) to address compliance with these principles and detection and correction of any non-compliance.

(5) Training

In connection with its commitment to enforce and uphold the principles set forth in the Code, the Company provides training on recognizing the warning signs of human trafficking and slavery to those employees who have direct responsibility for supply chain management.

options.B: The financial ratio is 110/220 × 100 = 50%; 200% is its reciprocal calculation. Expertise warrants deference, not automatic acceptance. California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010

The Silgan Containers Supplier Code of Responsibility for Compliance with the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010

Silgan Containers maintains a valuable reputation in the business community for honesty and fair dealing by acting ethically and in accordance with the laws applicable to its business. It is Silgan's expectation that each of its suppliers will likewise conduct its business in a legal and ethical manner.

The California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010 ("California Law") addresses issues of slavery and human trafficking, which are crimes under state, federal and international laws. In support of this law, Silgan requires that its major manufacturing suppliers comply with their obligations under the California Law. Specifically, in supply agreements executed after the effective date of the California Law, Silgan requires certification of compliance with the California Law by those suppliers that are covered by the law, and that the supplier comply with laws regarding slavery and human trafficking in the countries in which the supplier produces its products. Silgan verifies such compliance in periodic contractual compliance audits that Silgan conducts. At times of contract renewals, Silgan reviews the certifications from these suppliers as it assesses their performance and determines which suppliers it will continue to do business with. Thus, Silgan maintains internal standards and procedures for its employees and contractors that fail to meet Silgan's standards regarding slavery and human trafficking. Silgan conducts training sessions on a periodic basis for Silgan purchasing managers with respect to the California Law.

CORPORATE RESPONSIBILITY

True Religion Apparel, Inc. Corporate Responsibility



True Religion Apparel, Inc., together with its subsidiaries and affiliates (collectively, the “Company”), is dedicated to upholding fair and legal employment practices and environmental sustainability requirements.

As an integral component of this commitment, we have developed and implemented an Associate Code of Conduct (the “Code,” available here), which applies to all vendors, manufacturers, contractors, and suppliers (“Associates”) that form a part of our supply chain.

The Code advises our Associates of their obligation to adhere to all applicable local, state (including the California Transparency in Supply Chain Act) and federal laws as well as the standards established by the Company and set forth in the Code.

The core elements of our Code are prohibitions on discrimination, forced labor, and child labor, insistence on fair wages and hours and the provision of safe and healthy working conditions, as well as guidelines for minimizing each Associate’s environmental footprint.

As a condition of doing business with the Company, each Associate must execute the Code and implement the principles contained therein.

The Company will continue to develop Associate monitoring systems including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced third party audits to assess and ensure compliance with the Code.

If the Company determines that any Associate has violated the Code, the Company may either terminate its business relationship or require the Associate to implement a corrective action plan.

By espousing the foregoing principles, the Company strives to ensure integrity of its supply chain while continuing to uphold and exceed the quality of our branded merchandise.



2012 California Transparency in Supply Chain Act (SB 657) (the “Act”)

The Act, which became effective January 1, 2012, requires certain retail sellers and manufacturers to disclose their efforts to eradicate slavery and human trafficking from their direct supply chains. It is intended to provide consumers with the means to determine which companies have an active social responsibility program and thereafter to make conscientious purchasing decisions.

The points outlined below highlight the Act’s mandatory disclosures, followed by an explanation of how the Company is addressing each of them:

(1) Verification

The Company continues to develop monitoring systems to assess and ensure Associate’s compliance with the slavery and human trafficking prohibitions set forth in the Code through various means, including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced on-site third party verification visits.

(2) Audits

The Company relies on independent third party vendors to conducts unannounced audits of Associates, which assist in the evaluation of Associates’ compliance with Company’s supply chain standards for trafficking and slavery.

(3) Integrity of Components

By executing the Code, every Associate certifies that materials incorporated into goods and merchandise manufactured for the Company comply with labor and trafficking laws, and with all other applicable laws, rules and regulations of the respective country or countries in which they do business.

(4) Accountability

Associates must manifest their commitment to the implementation of the Code’s stated anti-slavery and human trafficking principles by maintaining or establishing an appropriate management system (with adequate documentation and record-keeping in place) to address compliance with these principles and detection and correction of any non-compliance.

(5) Training

In connection with its commitment to enforce and uphold the principles set forth in the Code, the Company provides training on recognizing the warning signs of human trafficking and slavery to those employees who have direct responsibility for supply chain management.

True Religion Apparel, Inc. Corporate Responsibility



True Religion Apparel, Inc., together with its subsidiaries and affiliates (collectively, the “Company”), is dedicated to upholding fair and legal employment practices and environmental sustainability requirements.

As an integral component of this commitment, we have developed and implemented an Associate Code of Conduct (the “Code,” available here), which applies to all vendors, manufacturers, contractors, and suppliers (“Associates”) that form a part of our supply chain.

The Code advises our Associates of their obligation to adhere to all applicable local, state (including the California Transparency in Supply Chain Act) and federal laws as well as the standards established by the Company and set forth in the Code.

The core elements of our Code are prohibitions on discrimination, forced labor, and child labor, insistence on fair wages and hours and the provision of safe and healthy working conditions, as well as guidelines for minimizing each Associate’s environmental footprint.

As a condition of doing business with the Company, each Associate must execute the Code and implement the principles contained therein.

The Company will continue to develop Associate monitoring systems including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced third party audits to assess and ensure compliance with the Code.

If the Company determines that any Associate has violated the Code, the Company may either terminate its business relationship or require the Associate to implement a corrective action plan.

By espousing the foregoing principles, the Company strives to ensure integrity of its supply chain while continuing to uphold and exceed the quality of our branded merchandise.



2012 California Transparency in Supply Chain Act (SB 657) (the “Act”)

The Act, which became effective January 1, 2012, requires certain retail sellers and manufacturers to disclose their efforts to eradicate slavery and human trafficking from their direct supply chains. It is intended to provide consumers with the means to determine which companies have an active social responsibility program and thereafter to make conscientious purchasing decisions.

The points outlined below highlight the Act’s mandatory disclosures, followed by an explanation of how the Company is addressing each of them:

(1) Verification

The Company continues to develop monitoring systems to assess and ensure Associate’s compliance with the slavery and human trafficking prohibitions set forth in the Code through various means, including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced on-site third party verification visits.

(2) Audits

The Company relies on independent third party vendors to conducts unannounced audits of Associates, which assist in the evaluation of Associates’ compliance with Company’s supply chain standards for trafficking and slavery.

(3) Integrity of Components

By executing the Code, every Associate certifies that materials incorporated into goods and merchandise manufactured for the Company comply with labor and trafficking laws, and with all other applicable laws, rules and regulations of the respective country or countries in which they do business.

(4) Accountability

Associates must manifest their commitment to the implementation of the Code’s stated anti-slavery and human trafficking principles by maintaining or establishing an appropriate management system (with adequate documentation and record-keeping in place) to address compliance with these principles and detection and correction of any non-compliance.

(5) Training

In connection with its commitment to enforce and uphold the principles set forth in the Code, the Company provides training on recognizing the warning signs of human trafficking and slavery to those employees who have direct responsibility for supply chain management.

The Silgan Containers Supplier Code of Responsibility for Compliance with the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010

Silgan Containers maintains a valuable reputation in the business community for honesty and fair dealing by acting ethically and in accordance with the laws applicable to its business. In support of this law, Silgan requires that its major manufacturing suppliers comply with their obligations under the California Law. At times of contract renewals, Silgan reviews the certifications from these suppliers as it assesses their performance and determines which suppliers it will continue to do business with. Thus, Silgan maintains internal standards and procedures for its employees and contractors that fail to meet Silgan's standards regarding slavery and human trafficking. Silgan conducts training sessions on a periodic basis for Silgan purchasing managers with respect to the California Law.

CORPORATE RESPONSIBILITY

True Religion Apparel, Inc. Corporate Responsibility



True Religion Apparel, Inc., together with its subsidiaries and affiliates (collectively, the “Company”), is dedicated to upholding fair and legal employment practices and environmental sustainability requirements.

As an integral component of this commitment, we have developed and implemented an Associate Code of Conduct (the “Code,” available here), which applies to all vendors, manufacturers, contractors, and suppliers (“Associates”) that form a part of our supply chain.

The Code advises our Associates of their obligation to adhere to all applicable local, state (including the California Transparency in Supply Chain Act) and federal laws as well as the standards established by the Company and set forth in the Code.

The core elements of our Code are prohibitions on discrimination, forced labor, and child labor, insistence on fair wages and hours and the provision of safe and healthy working conditions, as well as guidelines for minimizing each Associate’s environmental footprint.

As a condition of doing business with the Company, each Associate must execute the Code and implement the principles contained therein.

The Company will continue to develop Associate monitoring systems including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced third party audits to assess and ensure compliance with the Code.

If the Company determines that any Associate has violated the Code, the Company may either terminate its business relationship or require the Associate to implement a corrective action plan.

By espousing the foregoing principles, the Company strives to ensure integrity of its supply chain while continuing to uphold and exceed the quality of our branded merchandise.



2012 California Transparency in Supply Chain Act (SB 657) (the “Act”)

The Act, which became effective January 1, 2012, requires certain retail sellers and manufacturers to disclose their efforts to eradicate slavery and human trafficking from their direct supply chains. It is intended to provide consumers with the means to determine which companies have an active social responsibility program and thereafter to make conscientious purchasing decisions.

The points outlined below highlight the Act’s mandatory disclosures, followed by an explanation of how the Company is addressing each of them:

(1) Verification

The Company continues to develop monitoring systems to assess and ensure Associate’s compliance with the slavery and human trafficking prohibitions set forth in the Code through various means, including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced on-site third party verification visits.

(2) Audits

The Company relies on independent third party vendors to conducts unannounced audits of Associates, which assist in the evaluation of Associates’ compliance with Company’s supply chain standards for trafficking and slavery.

(3) Integrity of Components

By executing the Code, every Associate certifies that materials incorporated into goods and merchandise manufactured for the Company comply with labor and trafficking laws, and with all other applicable laws, rules and regulations of the respective country or countries in which they do business.

(4) Accountability

Associates must manifest their commitment to the implementation of the Code’s stated anti-slavery and human trafficking principles by maintaining or establishing an appropriate management system (with adequate documentation and record-keeping in place) to address compliance with these principles and detection and correction of any non-compliance.

(5) Training

In connection with its commitment to enforce and uphold the principles set forth in the Code, the Company provides training on recognizing the warning signs of human trafficking and slavery to those employees who have direct responsibility for supply chain management.

California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010

The Silgan Containers Supplier Code of Responsibility for Compliance with the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010

Silgan Containers maintains a valuable reputation in the business community for honesty and fair dealing by acting ethically and in accordance with the laws applicable to its business. It is Silgan's expectation that each of its suppliers will likewise conduct its business in a legal and ethical manner.

The California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010 ("California Law") addresses issues of slavery and human trafficking, which are crimes under state, federal and international laws. In support of this law, Silgan requires that its major manufacturing suppliers comply with their obligations under the California Law. Specifically, in supply agreements executed after the effective date of the California Law, Silgan requires certification of compliance with the California Law by those suppliers that are covered by the law, and that the supplier comply with laws regarding slavery and human trafficking in the countries in which the supplier produces its products. Silgan verifies such compliance in periodic contractual compliance audits that Silgan conducts. At times of contract renewals, Silgan reviews the certifications from these suppliers as it assesses their performance and determines which suppliers it will continue to do business with. Thus, Silgan maintains internal standards and procedures for its employees and contractors that fail to meet Silgan's standards regarding slavery and human trafficking. Silgan conducts training sessions on a periodic basis for Silgan purchasing managers with respect to the California Law.

CORPORATE RESPONSIBILITY

True Religion Apparel, Inc. Corporate Responsibility



True Religion Apparel, Inc., together with its subsidiaries and affiliates (collectively, the “Company”), is dedicated to upholding fair and legal employment practices and environmental sustainability requirements.

As an integral component of this commitment, we have developed and implemented an Associate Code of Conduct (the “Code,” available here), which applies to all vendors, manufacturers, contractors, and suppliers (“Associates”) that form a part of our supply chain.

The Code advises our Associates of their obligation to adhere to all applicable local, state (including the California Transparency in Supply Chain Act) and federal laws as well as the standards established by the Company and set forth in the Code.

The core elements of our Code are prohibitions on discrimination, forced labor, and child labor, insistence on fair wages and hours and the provision of safe and healthy working conditions, as well as guidelines for minimizing each Associate’s environmental footprint.

As a condition of doing business with the Company, each Associate must execute the Code and implement the principles contained therein.

The Company will continue to develop Associate monitoring systems including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced third party audits to assess and ensure compliance with the Code.

If the Company determines that any Associate has violated the Code, the Company may either terminate its business relationship or require the Associate to implement a corrective action plan.

By espousing the foregoing principles, the Company strives to ensure integrity of its supply chain while continuing to uphold and exceed the quality of our branded merchandise.



2012 California Transparency in Supply Chain Act (SB 657) (the “Act”)

The Act, which became effective January 1, 2012, requires certain retail sellers and manufacturers to disclose their efforts to eradicate slavery and human trafficking from their direct supply chains. It is intended to provide consumers with the means to determine which companies have an active social responsibility program and thereafter to make conscientious purchasing decisions.

The points outlined below highlight the Act’s mandatory disclosures, followed by an explanation of how the Company is addressing each of them:

(1) Verification

The Company continues to develop monitoring systems to assess and ensure Associate’s compliance with the slavery and human trafficking prohibitions set forth in the Code through various means, including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced on-site third party verification visits.

(2) Audits

The Company relies on independent third party vendors to conducts unannounced audits of Associates, which assist in the evaluation of Associates’ compliance with Company’s supply chain standards for trafficking and slavery.

(3) Integrity of Components

By executing the Code, every Associate certifies that materials incorporated into goods and merchandise manufactured for the Company comply with labor and trafficking laws, and with all other applicable laws, rules and regulations of the respective country or countries in which they do business.

(4) Accountability

Associates must manifest their commitment to the implementation of the Code’s stated anti-slavery and human trafficking principles by maintaining or establishing an appropriate management system (with adequate documentation and record-keeping in place) to address compliance with these principles and detection and correction of any non-compliance.

(5) Training

In connection with its commitment to enforce and uphold the principles set forth in the Code, the Company provides training on recognizing the warning signs of human trafficking and slavery to those employees who have direct responsibility for supply chain management.

question: A direct financial institution is preparing a client-facing due-diligence note. Silgan discloses that supply agreements executed after the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act's effective date require covered major manufacturing suppliers to certify compliance with that law and comply with slavery and human-trafficking laws in their production countries. Silgan conducts periodic contractual compliance audits and reviews certifications at renewal. Which note best identifies the institution's principal service audience and concludes whether Silgan discloses supplier-certification requirements, their scope, applicable laws, and compliance checks?

options.A: For investors: Silgan expects suppliers to conduct business legally and ethically. Its commitment to honesty and fair dealing is the relevant conclusion for this due-diligence note.
options.B: For investors: Yes, Silgan discloses certification requirements for covered major manufacturing suppliers under post-effective-date agreements, production-country legal compliance, periodic Silgan audits, and renewal certification reviews. These are disclosed requirements and checks, not proof that violations never occur.
options.C: Finance reference: Direct financial institutions principally serve investors. Separate supplier-policy reference: Covered major manufacturing suppliers certify under post-effective-date agreements, comply with production-country laws, undergo periodic Silgan audits, and have certifications reviewed at renewal.
options.D: For investors: Silgan's disclosure establishes your eligibility requirements for direct financing: certify compliance with slavery and human-trafficking laws in production countries under post-effective-date agreements, submit to periodic Silgan audits, and renew your certifications.

explanation: Direct financial institutions principally serve investors. Silgan's disclosure supports an affirmative supplier-certification disclosure assessment, limited to covered major manufacturing suppliers and agreements executed after the law's effective date. It identifies production-country slavery and human-trafficking laws, periodic contractual compliance audits conducted by Silgan, and certification reviews at renewal. Disclosing these requirements and processes does not establish that violations never occur.

distractor_analysis.reason: It identifies investors correctly but substitutes a generic ethical commitment for the required assessment of certification scope, applicable laws, and compliance checks.

It accurately lists financial and supplier-policy facts separately but does not integrate them into an investor-facing conclusion about whether the disclosure establishes supplier-certification requirements.
It incorrectly transfers obligations imposed on covered suppliers to investors and treats supplier oversight as an eligibility condition for direct financing.

CORPORATE RESPONSIBILITY

True Religion Apparel, Inc. Corporate Responsibility



True Religion Apparel, Inc., together with its subsidiaries and affiliates (collectively, the “Company”), is dedicated to upholding fair and legal employment practices and environmental sustainability requirements.

As an integral component of this commitment, we have developed and implemented an Associate Code of Conduct (the “Code,” available here), which applies to all vendors, manufacturers, contractors, and suppliers (“Associates”) that form a part of our supply chain.

The Code advises our Associates of their obligation to adhere to all applicable local, state (including the California Transparency in Supply Chain Act) and federal laws as well as the standards established by the Company and set forth in the Code.

The core elements of our Code are prohibitions on discrimination, forced labor, and child labor, insistence on fair wages and hours and the provision of safe and healthy working conditions, as well as guidelines for minimizing each Associate’s environmental footprint.

As a condition of doing business with the Company, each Associate must execute the Code and implement the principles contained therein.

The Company will continue to develop Associate monitoring systems including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced third party audits to assess and ensure compliance with the Code.

If the Company determines that any Associate has violated the Code, the Company may either terminate its business relationship or require the Associate to implement a corrective action plan.

By espousing the foregoing principles, the Company strives to ensure integrity of its supply chain while continuing to uphold and exceed the quality of our branded merchandise.



2012 California Transparency in Supply Chain Act (SB 657) (the “Act”)

The Act, which became effective January 1, 2012, requires certain retail sellers and manufacturers to disclose their efforts to eradicate slavery and human trafficking from their direct supply chains. It is intended to provide consumers with the means to determine which companies have an active social responsibility program and thereafter to make conscientious purchasing decisions.

The points outlined below highlight the Act’s mandatory disclosures, followed by an explanation of how the Company is addressing each of them:

(1) Verification

The Company continues to develop monitoring systems to assess and ensure Associate’s compliance with the slavery and human trafficking prohibitions set forth in the Code through various means, including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced on-site third party verification visits.

(2) Audits

The Company relies on independent third party vendors to conducts unannounced audits of Associates, which assist in the evaluation of Associates’ compliance with Company’s supply chain standards for trafficking and slavery.

(3) Integrity of Components

By executing the Code, every Associate certifies that materials incorporated into goods and merchandise manufactured for the Company comply with labor and trafficking laws, and with all other applicable laws, rules and regulations of the respective country or countries in which they do business.

(4) Accountability

Associates must manifest their commitment to the implementation of the Code’s stated anti-slavery and human trafficking principles by maintaining or establishing an appropriate management system (with adequate documentation and record-keeping in place) to address compliance with these principles and detection and correction of any non-compliance.

(5) Training

In connection with its commitment to enforce and uphold the principles set forth in the Code, the Company provides training on recognizing the warning signs of human trafficking and slavery to those employees who have direct responsibility for supply chain management.

question: A direct financial institution is preparing a client-facing due-diligence note. Silgan discloses that supply agreements executed after the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act's effective date require covered major manufacturing suppliers to certify compliance with that Act and comply with slavery and human-trafficking laws in their production countries. Silgan conducts periodic contractual compliance audits and reviews certifications at contract renewal. Which note identifies the institution's principal service audience and concludes whether Silgan discloses supplier-certification requirements, their scope, applicable laws, and compliance checks?

options.A: For investors: Silgan's stated commitment to lawful and ethical supplier conduct provides the relevant due-diligence conclusion. Its expectations of suppliers demonstrate an ethical approach to slavery and human-trafficking concerns.
options.B: For investors: Yes—the disclosure describes certification under the California Act for covered major manufacturing suppliers in post-effective-date agreements, production-country slavery and human-trafficking compliance, periodic contractual audits, and renewal certification reviews. These are disclosed requirements and checks, not proof that violations never occur.
options.C: Direct financial institutions principally serve investors. Separately, Silgan describes California Act certification for covered major manufacturing suppliers in post-effective-date agreements, production-country slavery and human-trafficking compliance, periodic contractual audits, and renewal certification reviews. No conclusion is offered on what this disclosure establishes for the client note.
options.D: For investors: Yes—the disclosure establishes certification conditions for participation in direct financing. Investors must satisfy the covered suppliers' California Act and production-country slavery and human-trafficking requirements and undergo Silgan's periodic audits and renewal certification reviews before investing.

explanation: Direct financial institutions principally serve investors. Silgan's disclosure supports an affirmative supplier-certification disclosure assessment: it identifies covered major manufacturing suppliers, limits the relevant agreements to those executed after the Act's effective date, specifies compliance with production-country slavery and human-trafficking laws, and describes periodic contractual audits and certification reviews at renewal. The note properly reports disclosed requirements and oversight rather than guaranteeing actual compliance or extending supplier obligations to investors.

distractor_analysis.reason: It identifies the correct audience but substitutes general ethical expectations for an assessment of certification requirements, scope, applicable laws, and compliance checks.

It accurately states the financial audience and legal disclosure facts separately, but expressly omits the requested investor-facing conclusion about whether the disclosure establishes supplier-certification requirements and oversight.

It incorrectly transfers supplier obligations and Silgan's supplier compliance checks to investors as conditions of direct-financing participation. Being the institution's service audience does not make investors subject to those supplier requirements.

question_plan: Audit the source's claim that a Chinese one-year time deposit earning 2.50% with CPI inflation of 3.80% has a real annual return of −1.27%. Assuming these annual rates remain constant and all interest is reinvested on renewal, derive the deposit's purchasing-power multiplier after n years, explain its exponential form, and use n = 1 to check the claimed percentage.

answer_plans.plan: Reinvested interest applies to the current balance, giving nominal growth P(1.025)^n; the price-level multiplier is (1.038)^n. Divide to obtain purchasing power P(1.025/1.038)^n in initial-year money, an exponential decline. For one year, the real return is (1.025/1.038 − 1) × 100% ≈ −1.2524%, rounding to −1.25%. Explicitly identify the source's keyed −1.27% as inconsistent with exact adjustment.
Correctly model reinvestment as P(1.025)^n but treat this nominal balance as purchasing power. Report a positive 2.50% annual real return because the financial need to adjust for CPI is omitted.

Explain exponential percentage growth and separately calculate the nominal balance P(1.025)^n and price multiplier (1.038)^n. State that inflation reduces purchasing power, but never divide the two growth factors, leaving the real-return claim unaudited.

Reverse the adjustment ratio and use (1.038/1.025)^n as the purchasing-power multiplier. Report approximately +1.27% for one year, incorrectly interpreting price growth relative to deposit growth as a gain in the deposit's purchasing power.

mathematics.necessity: Reinvested interest must apply to each renewed balance rather than repeatedly to the initial principal.
Constant annual percentage changes produce the n-year growth factors needed to model the deposit and price level.
The nominal-growth-to-price-growth fraction must be evaluated as division to calculate purchasing power and audit the one-year return.

question: A stock's percentage price change is positive. Let x be its signed dollar price change and y the corresponding put option's signed price change, with other pricing factors held constant. An analyst proposes y = kx, k > 0. Which assessment correctly identifies the model's quadrants, the expected change pair's quadrant, and the model's directional consistency?

options.A: Model: I and III; expected pair: I because both prices rise; consistent.
options.B: Model: I and III; expected pair: IV because the stock rises and the put falls; inconsistent.
options.C: Model: I and III; the stock rises and the put falls, but the pair's quadrant and model consistency cannot be determined.
options.D: Model: I and III; expected pair: I because the put's loss is a positive magnitude; consistent.

explanation: A positive percentage change means the stock increased, so x > 0. Holding other pricing factors constant, the put price falls, so y < 0. The expected pair therefore lies in quadrant IV. The line y = kx with k > 0 passes through quadrants I and III and predicts y > 0 when x > 0, contradicting the expected put-price direction. This does not establish that the true relationship is exactly linear.

distractor_analysis.reason: It correctly identifies the positive-slope model's quadrants but ignores the inverse stock–put price relationship, incorrectly predicting that the put rises.
It states the relevant financial and mathematical facts separately but fails to combine them: x > 0 and y < 0 determine quadrant IV and contradict the proposed model.
It replaces the put's signed price change with the positive magnitude of its loss. Since y is defined as a signed change, a falling put price requires y < 0.

question: Bing/MSN terms limit content to “noncommercial, personal use,” permit other uses only when specifically authorized by Microsoft or rights holders or allowed by copyright law, and reserve rights not expressly granted. A company proposes commercial reuse; assume no copyright-law permission applies. It then obtains a specifically authorized commercial-use license for $600,000, recognized as an intangible asset with a six-year useful life. No residual-value exception applies. Management claims commercial authorization automatically grants resale rights and supports a $60,000 residual value. Which assessment correctly addresses access, authorization, resale rights, residual value, and annual straight-line amortization, using (cost − residual value)/useful life?

options.A: Ordinary access is insufficient; specific authorization is required. Resale rights are not automatic, but use management’s $60,000 residual value and amortize $90,000 annually.
options.B: Ordinary access is insufficient; specific authorization is required. Resale rights are not automatic; use zero residual value and amortize $100,000 annually.
options.C: The terms restrict personal use, allow specifically authorized other uses, and reserve ungranted rights. Finite-life intangibles generally have zero residual value; these general rules alone are the assessment.
options.D: Ordinary access is insufficient; specific authorization is required. Although residual value is generally zero, commercial authorization automatically creates resale rights supporting $60,000 residual value and $90,000 annual amortization.

explanation: Ordinary access permits only noncommercial personal use. Without copyright-law permission, the company needs specific authorization from Microsoft or the rights holders for commercial reuse. Because ungranted rights are reserved, that authorization does not automatically include resale rights. The license is stipulated to be a finite-life intangible with no residual-value exception, so its residual value is generally zero. Annual straight-line amortization is ($600,000 − $0)/6 = $100,000.

distractor_analysis.reason: It correctly applies the authorization and reserved-rights provisions but accepts an unsupported residual value despite the zero-residual-value rule and the stated absence of an exception.
It lists relevant legal and accounting rules without applying them to the proposed reuse, management’s resale claim, or the license’s annual amortization.

It wrongly links commercial authorization to automatic resale rights and then treats those supposed rights as an accounting exception, contradicting both the reservation of ungranted rights and the stipulated absence of a residual-value exception.

question: Bing/MSN terms restrict content to “noncommercial, personal use only.” Other uses require specific authorization from Microsoft or rights holders, unless allowed by copyright law; rights not expressly granted are reserved. A company proposes commercial reuse, with no applicable copyright-law permission. If authorized, it will pay $600,000 for a commercial-use license, stipulated to be a recognized intangible asset with a six-year useful life. The license does not expressly grant resale rights, and no residual-value exception applies. Management claims commercial authorization automatically permits resale and supports a $60,000 residual value. Which assessment correctly addresses permission, resale rights, residual value, and annual straight-line amortization using (cost − residual value)/useful life?

options.A: Ordinary access is insufficient; specific authorization is required. Resale rights are not automatic, but management's $60,000 residual value is acceptable, giving $90,000 annual amortization.
options.B: Ordinary access is insufficient; specific authorization is required. Resale rights are not automatic; use zero residual value and $100,000 annual amortization.
options.C: The terms restrict ordinary access to personal use, allow specifically authorized uses, and reserve ungranted rights. Finite-life intangible assets generally have zero residual value; straight-line amortization equals depreciable cost divided by useful life.
options.D: Ordinary access is insufficient; specific authorization is required. Although residual value is generally zero, purchasing commercial authorization automatically grants resale rights and creates an exception: use $60,000 residual value and $90,000 annual amortization.

explanation: Ordinary access permits noncommercial personal use, not the proposed commercial reuse. With no copyright-law permission, the company needs specific authorization from Microsoft or the rights holders. Because ungranted rights are reserved, commercial-use authorization does not automatically confer resale rights. The recognized license has a finite useful life and no residual-value exception, so its residual value is generally zero. Annual straight-line amortization is ($600,000 − $0)/6 = $100,000.

distractor_analysis.reason: It correctly applies the permission and reserved-rights terms but accepts an unsupported residual value despite the finite-life rule and the stipulated absence of an exception. The $90,000 calculation therefore uses the wrong residual value.

It lists relevant legal and financial principles separately but does not decide whether the proposed reuse is permitted, assess management's resale claim, or determine the license's residual value and annual amortization.

It incorrectly links commercial-use authorization to automatic resale rights and an accounting exception. The terms reserve ungranted rights, and the question expressly excludes a residual-value exception.

question: Bing/MSN terms state that content is for “noncommercial, personal use only”; other uses require specific authorization from Microsoft or rights holders, or permission under applicable copyright law; ungranted rights are reserved. A company proposes commercial reuse, with no applicable copyright-law permission. If specifically authorized, it will purchase a $600,000 commercial-use license, stipulated to be a recognized intangible asset with a six-year useful life. No resale rights are expressly granted and no residual-value exception applies. Management claims commercial authorization automatically permits resale and supports a $60,000 residual value. Which assessment correctly resolves access, authorization, resale rights, and annual straight-line amortization, using (cost − residual value)/useful life?

options.A: Ordinary access is insufficient; specific authorization from Microsoft or rights holders is required. Resale rights are not automatic, but management's $60,000 residual value is acceptable; annual amortization is $90,000.
options.B: Ordinary access is insufficient; specific authorization from Microsoft or rights holders is required. Resale rights are not automatic; residual value is zero and annual amortization is $100,000.
options.C: The terms restrict use to personal, noncommercial purposes, allow specifically authorized uses, and reserve ungranted rights. Finite-life intangibles generally have zero residual value; these rules alone leave this proposal's permissions and amortization unresolved.
options.D: Ordinary access is insufficient; specific authorization from Microsoft or rights holders is required. Although finite-life intangibles generally have zero residual value, buying commercial authorization creates resale rights and an exception; annual amortization is $90,000.

explanation: Ordinary access does not authorize the proposed commercial reuse. Because copyright-law permission is excluded, specific authorization from Microsoft or the rights holders is needed. The reservation of ungranted rights prevents treating that authorization as an automatic grant of resale rights. Separately, the license is stipulated to be a finite-life intangible with no residual-value exception, so its residual value is zero. Annual straight-line amortization is ($600,000 − $0)/6 = $100,000. Management's claim establishes neither resale rights nor a basis for a $60,000 residual value.

distractor_analysis.reason: It correctly applies the permission and reserved-rights terms but accepts an unsupported residual value despite the finite useful life and explicit absence of any residual-value exception. The $90,000 calculation uses the wrong amortizable amount.

It recites relevant legal and accounting rules without applying them to the proposal. The stated conditions are sufficient to determine the required authorization, reject automatic resale rights, and calculate $100,000 annual amortization.

It incorrectly links commercial-use authorization to an automatic resale entitlement and then to an accounting exception. Ungranted rights remain reserved, and the question expressly excludes a residual-value exception.

question: An enterprise's annual sales are $360,000 and grow by 1% of the preceding year's sales in each of the next two years. question: An applicant for a personal commercial property loan has paid $400,000 down and meets all other eligibility requirements. The property's final market value will be exactly $600,000, $800,000, or $1,000,000, with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, and 0.3, respectively. Policy requires a down payment of at least 50% of market value. Which option gives the probability that the existing payment meets this requirement and identifies the probability rule used?

options.A: 100%, by the law of total probability using a 30% minimum down payment.
options.B: The minimum payment is 50% of market value; the law of total probability is P(A) = Σᵢ P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ).
options.C: 70%, by the law of total probability over the three valuation scenarios.
options.D: 0%, by comparing the payment with 50% of the probability-weighted average valuation.

explanation: The required down payments are $300,000, $400,000, and $500,000. The existing $400,000 qualifies in the first two scenarios, since the 50% minimum includes equality, but not in the third. These mutually exclusive, exhaustive scenarios form a partition. Conditional qualification probabilities are therefore 1, 1, and 0. The law of total probability gives 1 × 0.2 + 1 × 0.5 + 0 × 0.3 = 0.7, or 70%.

distractor_analysis.reason: It applies total probability to eligibility classifications based on an incorrect 30% minimum. The required minimum is 50% of market value, so the $1,000,000 scenario does not qualify.
It states the financial threshold and probability formula separately but does not connect them by determining conditional qualification probabilities or provide the requested numerical probability.

The probability-weighted average valuation is $820,000, whose 50% threshold is $410,000. Failing this average-based threshold does not imply zero probability of qualification. The threshold must be applied within each valuation scenario before the resulting qualification probabilities are weighted.

question: Alice is entitled to an exemption for 2018, but the applicable statute defines the exemption amount as zero for taxable years beginning in 2018–2025. A cross-jurisdiction tax-help article claims this means no tax is payable and no filing is required, making simplified filing or consolidated tax periods unnecessary for regular fixed-amount taxpayers under a separate jurisdiction's tax-administration rules. Which audit correctly addresses the statute and the article's inference? Do not assume Alice is a regular fixed-amount taxpayer.

options.A: Alice's entitlement guarantees a positive exemption amount. Under the separate rules, no tax payable does not remove filing duties, and regular fixed-amount taxpayers may use simplified filing and consolidated tax periods.
options.B: Alice's exemption amount is zero, which establishes neither zero tax payable nor relief from filing. Under the separate rules, even no tax payable does not remove filing duties; regular fixed-amount taxpayers may use simplified filing and consolidated tax periods.
options.C: Alice's exemption amount is zero, and regular fixed-amount taxpayers may use simplified filing and consolidated tax periods. These separate facts suffice for the audit without addressing whether zero amounts remove filing duties.
options.D: Alice's exemption amount is zero, so no tax is payable. This zero-amount rule overrides the separate filing duties, allowing regular fixed-amount taxpayers to omit filings instead of using simplified filing or consolidated tax periods.

explanation: The statutory special rule applies to 2018, so Alice's exemption amount is zero despite her stated entitlement. An exemption amount is not a determination of tax payable or filing duties. Under the separate tax-administration rules, even taxpayers with no tax payable must file, while regular fixed-amount taxpayers may use simplified filing and consolidated tax periods. Neither rule establishes that Alice belongs to that taxpayer category.

question: Over the same interval, stock returns in regime A are −0.01 or 0.01 with equal probability; in regime B they are −0.02 or 0.02 with equal probability. Define volatility as the square root of return variance. Under standard option-pricing assumptions, with all other pricing inputs fixed, which option gives both regimes’ (variance, volatility) and the effect of switching from A to B on vanilla American and European calls and puts?

options.A: A: (0, 0); B: (0, 0). Higher volatility raises all four option values, but switching regimes leaves them unchanged.
options.B: A: (0.0001, 0.01); B: (0.0004, 0.02). Switching regimes raises all four option values.
options.C: A: (0.0001, 0.01); B: (0.0004, 0.02). Higher volatility raises all four option values; the effect of switching regimes is not specified.
options.D: A: (0.0001, 0.01); B: (0.0004, 0.02). Switching regimes raises both call values and lowers both put values.

explanation: Both return distributions have mean zero. Variance is the expected squared deviation from the mean, so A’s variance is 0.5(−0.01)² + 0.5(0.01)² = 0.0001, and B’s is 0.0004. Taking square roots gives volatilities of 0.01 and 0.02. With other pricing inputs fixed, higher stock-price volatility increases the value of calls and puts under both American and European exercise styles.

question: Over the same interval, stock returns in regime A are −0.01 or 0.01 with equal probability; in regime B, they are −0.02 or 0.02 with equal probability. Define volatility as the square root of return variance. Holding all other pricing inputs fixed under standard option-pricing assumptions, which choice correctly gives each regime’s (variance, volatility) and explicitly states the predicted effect of switching from A to B on vanilla American and European calls and puts?

options.A: A: (0, 0); B: (0, 0). Higher volatility raises option values, but this switch leaves all four values unchanged.
options.B: A: (0.0001, 0.01); B: (0.0004, 0.02). The switch raises call and put values under both exercise styles.
options.C: A: (0.0001, 0.01); B: (0.0004, 0.02). In general, volatility is positively related to call and put values under both exercise styles.
options.D: A: (0.0001, 0.01); B: (0.0004, 0.02). The switch raises call values but lowers put values under both exercise styles.

explanation: Both regimes have mean return zero. Variance is E[(X − E(X))²], so A’s variance is 0.5(−0.01)² + 0.5(0.01)² = 0.0001, while B’s is 0.0004. Taking square roots gives volatilities of 0.01 and 0.02. Thus, switching to B increases volatility. With other pricing inputs fixed, the positive volatility–option value relationship predicts higher values for both calls and puts, whether American or European.

distractor_analysis.reason: It averages unsquared deviations, which cancel to zero, instead of squared deviations. This incorrectly makes both volatilities zero and leads to the unchanged-value conclusion.
It provides correct calculations and a correct general financial relationship separately, but does not explicitly apply that relationship to state the effect of switching from A to B, as requested.
Its calculations are correct, but it incorrectly maps higher volatility to lower put values. The positive volatility relationship applies to puts as well as calls under both exercise styles.

question: Investigators intercept 100 students at a cafeteria entrance to record monthly consumption expenditures x_i. Define A1 = (1/100)∑x_i and A2 = (1/100)∑x_i². An analyst substitutes these for the first two population raw moments, claiming that A2 estimates variance and that this procedure makes the sample simple random. Which assessment fully corrects the claims, naming both methods and giving the proposed mean and variance estimates?

options.A: Convenience sampling; mean estimate A1 and variance estimate A2. The estimation method is unspecified, and recruitment remains convenience sampling.
options.B: Convenience sampling; method of moments; mean estimate A1 and variance estimate A2 − A1². Estimation does not change the sampling classification.
options.C: Convenience sampling; method of moments substitutes sample moments for population moments. Variance is the expected squared deviation from the population mean.
options.D: Initially convenience sampling; method of moments; mean estimate A1 and variance estimate A2 − A1². Moment matching converts it into simple random sampling.

explanation: Intercepting students at the cafeteria entrance is convenience sampling. Replacing population moments with sample moments is the method of moments. The mean is E[X], giving estimate A1. Expanding Var(X) = E[(X − E[X])²] gives E[X²] − (E[X])², so the proposed variance estimate is A2 − A1². A2 alone estimates the second raw moment. These calculations do not change how students were recruited or make the sample random.

distractor_analysis.reason: It correctly identifies convenience sampling but fails to recognize the method of moments and confuses the second raw moment with variance.
Its separate definitions are correct, but it neither applies them to obtain the estimates from A1 and A2 nor resolves the claim that estimation changes the sampling classification.

It correctly names the methods and gives the moment-based estimates, but incorrectly links moment matching to random recruitment. Estimation cannot convert convenience sampling into simple random sampling.

question: Gold costs $1200/ounce, annual storage costs 2% of the initial spot price payable at year-end, the one-year risk-free rate is 6%, and one-year futures trade at $1350/ounce. Futures are cash-settled at maturity, when the gold is sold at S_T. Assume no other costs or interim margin cash flows. Each proposal buys one ounce of gold and shorts risk-free government bonds for $1200 of initial proceeds. Which proposal completes a self-financing arbitrage and establishes its spot-price-independent terminal profit? Let G denote the financed gold leg's net terminal cash flow and H the futures payoff.

options.A: Short one ounce of futures; G = S_T − 1272, H = 1350 − S_T; G + H = $78.
options.B: Short one ounce of futures; G = S_T − 1296, H = 1350 − S_T. Separately, x + y = 3 and −x + y = 1 yield 2y = 4.
options.C: Short one ounce of futures; G = S_T − 1296, H = 1350 − S_T; G + H = $54.
options.D: Go long one ounce of futures; G = S_T − 1296, H = S_T − 1350; G + H = $54.

explanation: Shorting the bonds raises the $1200 needed to buy the gold, so initial net cash flow is zero. At maturity, the bond obligation is 1200 × 1.06 = $1272 and storage costs 1200 × 0.02 = $24. Thus G = S_T − 1296. Short futures pay H = 1350 − S_T. Adding the equations eliminates S_T because its coefficients are opposite: G + H = S_T − 1296 + 1350 − S_T = $54. This positive payoff is independent of the terminal gold price.

distractor_analysis.reason: The trade directions and variable elimination are correct, but the gold leg omits the $24 year-end storage charge, overstating profit by $24.
It gives the correct financial cash flows and demonstrates valid elimination on unrelated equations, but never combines G and H to establish the portfolio's fixed terminal profit.
With long futures, both cash flows have coefficient +1 on S_T. Adding them produces 2S_T − 2646, not $54. Equal coefficients do not cancel under addition, so this position is exposed to gold prices.

In order to tell this story right I’ll section my post.   **Background:**  Relevant parties: Myself (f25), Mother (49), Brother (20), father (deceased), half-sister (no contact), half bother (no contact), my uncle who is protector (some contact but not close).  My parents were never married but had been together for 10 years. Previous to this my father was married and had two children. They divorced a few years before meeting my mother.  My father had a trust fund set up in in 1991 (before my brother and I were born but when my parents were together). My parents moved from the UK to another country were they made a life together – owning a property together, a boat and were in the process of building another property. Around 1996 my father sold his business in the UK.  The unbuilt house, the business and the boat were all assets of the trust.  My father passed away unexpectedly back in 1998 when I was around the age of five and my brother (M20) was a few months old.   **History of the Trust:**  The 1991 Deed The trust was set up in 1991 – the original trustees were UK residents. The trust was established by a deed of settlement and expressed to be a Guernsey law trust. The protector of the trust was appointed to my uncle.  The beneficiaries of the trust were declared: 1. The settlor (life tenant) 2. The spouse and any former spouse of the settlor 3. The children of the settlor.  Change of trustees 1991 The trustees retired in favour of a new trust to take over.  1997 Deed 1 – Addition of my mother: My mother was added as a beneficiary.  1997 Deed 2: This introduced different terms. To pay the income of the trust to his children and my mother in equal shares until my brother reached 25, when of which all the capital will be divided between the beneficiaries.  1999 Appointment: Additions of beneficiaries and appointment of assets A deed was prepared that added myself and my brother as beneficiaries. This was due to them finding we do not come under the definition of children for the purposes of the trust or the 1997 Appointment as our parents were unmarried. This added new terms, notably allowing the discretionary distribution of income and capital before the youngest child (my brother) turned 25.  In order to be a part of this ‘deal’, my mother put my parents shared property in the trust portfolio (this is important information – bear with me!)  Change of Trustee 2002: The trustees retired in favour of a new trust to take over. This trust remains the current trustee of the trust.  2008 Deed: Appointments of the trust fund Under the 1999 deed the trust gave my half-sister and half-brother their full amounts as they are ‘legitimate’ children.   **The Problems:**  For years my family have had battles with the trust over unfair treatment. I wont go into the details of this, it’s so lengthy and an issue itself but we have asked to leave them a number of times. We were always told its not possible for any of us (Myself, Mother, Brother, Half-sister, Half-brother). We were told we would need to wait until my brother turned 25. Over the course of the years we’ve (my immediate family – not half siblings) lost about £60,000 + combined from fees.  Back in 2015, I asked for a deposit for my first home. After a lengthy email battle over the year, they finally agreed. At some point during this it came to light that my half siblings walked away years ago (we were never made aware), and that my mother has had the ability to walk away since 2008 (again, we were never told despite continuously asking to leave). When this came to light my mother instantly asked for her funds, they agreed to start making this happen.  It didn’t happen. Instead they sent us a letter a year later stating that after investigating our Trust as something came to light which means me and my brother may not be beneficiaries after all.  In preparing my distribution for my house deposit, they reviewed the 1991 Deed concerns were found/ raised.  **Problem 1**  Basically, my dad didn’t sign the ‘Change of trustees 1991’ document despite having priority power under the terms. It was executed by my uncle – as this dates way back we aren’t sure why, perhaps my father was unavailable. But he did instruct my uncle to do so on his behalf.  The second Trustees have communication from 1994 regarding this issue – however they, and the previous trustees decided they ‘were satisfied the Settlor was not available and therefor a change of trustees executed by the protector was valid’. This was because the settlement listed three person with the power to appoint replacements ‘The settelor, the protector and the trustees’  Flash forward 20 years and a law firm now thinks that the second trustees (1991) decision was ‘wrong’ and that our current trustees should take the matter to court seeking a clear idea of the tax consequences.  The law firm advice found there are two outcomes: 1.	The 1991 retirement deed is invalid but the 2002 deed is valid.  2.	Or they are both invalid and the trust should have never moved from the UK and there will be serious tax implications. There are serious tax implications for both and the trust are currently investigating these and we are awaiting results. This investigation is costly (£10,000 so far) and the distributions are being made from our ‘accounts’ with them.   **Problem 2: Me and my brother being added post 1991 Retirement Deed.**  As the 1991 Retirement Deed is likely to be found invalid, it is also likely me and my brother are invalid as this was exercised by ‘invalid’ trustees and after my fathers death. Yet my mothers appointment is fine as this was exercised by my father while he was alive and under the terms of the original 1991 deed.  Therefor we are awaiting tax information and investigation into the 1991 deed,1997 appointment and 1999 appointment as it has bearings on 1. The tax positions 2. The validity of past distributions 3. Whether to continue with court application 4. How to respond for future requests for distributions 5. Whether the second trust have any obligation to assist.  **Where we stand**  We’re currently awaiting the tax information but the trust have said to us that they would be looking at hopefully distributing all capital to us so we can walk away from this (yeah right – I’m sure they’re going to offer that).  From our point of view we are an innocent party to this. We’re angry that: 1. It seems we will have most of the capital taken from us due to mistakes that weren’t ours. 2. That they convinced my mother to put her shared home into the trust under a now false promise. 3. They may seek the past distributions from us! 4. Our half siblings have been able to walkaway from this mess.S o many other things.  **My main questions are:** 1.	Will we be held responsible and ultimately be the ones who will have to pay for this mess? 2.	Do you think there is any room to recoup loss/ sue for this mess (fees throughout the years and the likely loss of all the capital as this has not been picked up previously (apart from the communication in 1994)? 3.	If they do come back with a resolution to this (an offer to walkaway with a sum), do you think we should consider it? I’m concerned as I feel we are still the ones who have ultimately paid the price of someone else mistake. Even in the unlikely case this was presented, for all these years we have paid so many fees, and now feed for this tax/ law firm (who we have no contact with and know nothing about!) and the fact that my mother could have walked away years ago (she has been paying fees all that time!) 4.	What type of solicitor should we be seeking advice from?  Please help! This is causing us so much distress and pain. It’s been ongoing all my life and we just want out of it now.  TL;DR  Current Trust is arguing the previous trust was invalid as a retirement deed was signed by protector rather than my father who is now deceased. This makes previous addition of me and my brother (after my dad passed) invalid and the moving of the trust to a offshore trust invalid. This could have serious tax implications for us and also removes us from the trust, making all previous distributions invalid. Basically big £££ and distress over a mistake that was not ours and was overlooked for almost 20 years. Currently being made to pay all the legal costs of this by our trust (distributions being made from the trust capital). Should we sue or seek legal action?   Also half siblings were informed they could leave early and left in 2008 with capital. Despite my mother continuously asking to leave and being told no, it has recently come to light she could of in 2008 yet they didn’t tell her and she has paid fees since then!   Please, any advice is welcome :(   FYI Despite how this story sounds my father and mother came from different backgrounds – my mother being working class. I would consider us to be working class right now so available funds are limited and all tied up in the trust. Reply with either: Yes, No
