Post: My family are having issues with a trust fund set up by my father who passed away in 1998 and think we have been treated extremely unfairly for almost 20 years. This has now come to a breaking point – the trust has informed us they no longer think we (my brother and I) are beneficiaries due to an deed which was signed by Protector rather than my father and the firm are seeking legal and tax advice on the outcome of this.  In order to tell this story right I’ll section my post.   **Background:**  Relevant parties: Myself (f25), Mother (49), Brother (20), father (deceased), half-sister (no contact), half bother (no contact), my uncle who is protector (some contact but not close).  My parents were never married but had been together for 10 years. Previous to this my father was married and had two children. They divorced a few years before meeting my mother.  My father had a trust fund set up in in 1991 (before my brother and I were born but when my parents were together). My parents moved from the UK to another country were they made a life together – owning a property together, a boat and were in the process of building another property. Around 1996 my father sold his business in the UK.  The unbuilt house, the business and the boat were all assets of the trust.  My father passed away unexpectedly back in 1998 when I was around the age of five and my brother (M20) was a few months old.   **History of the Trust:**  The 1991 Deed The trust was set up in 1991 – the original trustees were UK residents. The trust was established by a deed of settlement and expressed to be a Guernsey law trust. The protector of the trust was appointed to my uncle.  The beneficiaries of the trust were declared: 1. The settlor (life tenant) 2. The spouse and any former spouse of the settlor 3. The children of the settlor.  Change of trustees 1991 The trustees retired in favour of a new trust to take over.  1997 Deed 1 – Addition of my mother: My mother was added as a beneficiary.  1997 Deed 2: This introduced different terms. To pay the income of the trust to his children and my mother in equal shares until my brother reached 25, when of which all the capital will be divided between the beneficiaries.  1999 Appointment: Additions of beneficiaries and appointment of assets A deed was prepared that added myself and my brother as beneficiaries. This was due to them finding we do not come under the definition of children for the purposes of the trust or the 1997 Appointment as our parents were unmarried. This added new terms, notably allowing the discretionary distribution of income and capital before the youngest child (my brother) turned 25.  In order to be a part of this ‘deal’, my mother put my parents shared property in the trust portfolio (this is important information – bear with me!)  Change of Trustee 2002: The trustees retired in favour of a new trust to take over. This trust remains the current trustee of the trust.  2008 Deed: Appointments of the trust fund Under the 1999 deed the trust gave my half-sister and half-brother their full amounts as they are ‘legitimate’ children.   **The Problems:**  For years my family have had battles with the trust over unfair treatment. I wont go into the details of this, it’s so lengthy and an issue itself but we have asked to leave them a number of times. We were always told its not possible for any of us (Myself, Mother, Brother, Half-sister, Half-brother). We were told we would need to wait until my brother turned 25. Over the course of the years we’ve (my immediate family – not half siblings) lost about £60,000 + combined from fees.  Back in 2015, I asked for a deposit for my first home. After a lengthy email battle over the year, they finally agreed. At some point during this it came to light that my half siblings walked away years ago (we were never made aware), and that my mother has had the ability to walk away since 2008 (again, we were never told despite continuously asking to leave). When this came to light my mother instantly asked for her funds, they agreed to start making this happen.  It didn’t happen. Instead they sent us a letter a year later stating that after investigating our Trust as something came to light which means me and my brother may not be beneficiaries after all.  In preparing my distribution for my house deposit, they reviewed the 1991 Deed concerns were found/ raised.  **Problem 1**  Basically, my dad didn’t sign the ‘Change of trustees 1991’ document despite having priority power under the terms. It was executed by my uncle – as this dates way back we aren’t sure why, perhaps my father was unavailable. But he did instruct my uncle to do so on his behalf.  The second Trustees have communication from 1994 regarding this issue – however they, and the previous trustees decided they ‘were satisfied the Settlor was not available and therefor a change of trustees executed by the protector was valid’. This was because the settlement listed three person with the power to appoint replacements ‘The settelor, the protector and the trustees’  Flash forward 20 years and a law firm now thinks that the second trustees (1991) decision was ‘wrong’ and that our current trustees should take the matter to court seeking a clear idea of the tax consequences.  The law firm advice found there are two outcomes: 1.	The 1991 retirement deed is invalid but the 2002 deed is valid.  2.	Or they are both invalid and the trust should have never moved from the UK and there will be serious tax implications. There are serious tax implications for both and the trust are currently investigating these and we are awaiting results. This investigation is costly (£10,000 so far) and the distributions are being made from our ‘accounts’ with them.   **Problem 2: Me and my brother being added post 1991 Retirement Deed.**  As the 1991 Retirement Deed is likely to be found invalid, it is also likely me and my brother are invalid as this was exercised by ‘invalid’ trustees and after my fathers death. Yet my mothers appointment is fine as this was exercised by my father while he was alive and under the terms of the original 1991 deed.  Therefor we are awaiting tax information and investigation into the 1991 deed,1997 appointment and 1999 appointment as it has bearings on 1. The tax positions 2. The validity of past distributions 3. Whether to continue with court application 4. How to respond for future requests for distributions 5. Whether the second trust have any obligation to assist.  **Where we stand**  We’re currently awaiting the tax information but the trust have said to us that they would be looking at hopefully distributing all capital to us so we can walk away from this (yeah right – I’m sure they’re going to offer that).  From our point of view we are an innocent party to this. We’re angry that: 1. It seems we will have most of the capital taken from us due to mistakes that weren’t ours. 2. That they convinced my mother to put her shared home into the trust under a now false promise. 3. They may seek the past distributions from us! 4. Our half siblings have been able to walkaway from this mess.S o many other things.  **My main questions are:** 1.	Will we be held responsible and ultimately be the ones who will have to pay for this mess? 2.	Do you think there is any room to recoup loss/ sue for this mess (fees throughout the years and the likely loss of all the capital as this has not been picked up previously (apart from the communication in 1994)? 3.	If they do come back with a resolution to this (an offer to walkaway with a sum), do you think we should consider it? I’m concerned as I feel we are still the ones who have ultimately paid the price of someone else mistake. Even in the unlikely case this was presented, for all these years we have paid so many fees, and now feed for this tax/ law firm (who we have no contact with and know nothing about!) and the fact that my mother could have walked away years ago (she has been paying fees all that time!) 4.	What type of solicitor should we be seeking advice from?  Please help! This is causing us so much distress and pain. It’s been ongoing all my life and we just want out of it now.  TL;DR  Current Trust is arguing the previous trust was invalid as a retirement deed was signed by protector rather than my father who is now deceased. This makes previous addition of me and my brother (after my dad passed) invalid and the moving of the trust to a offshore trust invalid. This could have serious tax implications for us and also removes us from the trust, making all previous distributions invalid. Basically big £££ and distress over a mistake that was not ours and was overlooked for almost 20 years. Currently being made to pay all the legal costs of this by our trust (distributions being made from the trust capital). Should we sue or seek legal action?   Also half siblings were informed they could leave early and left in 2008 with capital. Despite my mother continuously asking to leave and being told no, it has recently come to light she could of in 2008 yet they didn’t tell her and she has paid fees since then!   Please, any advice is welcome :(   FYI Despite how this story sounds my father and mother came from different backgrounds – my mother being working class. I would consider us to be working class right now so available funds are limited and all tied up in the trust. Reply with either: Yes, No

Post: My family are having issues with a trust fund set up by my father who passed away in 1998 and think we have been treated extremely unfairly for almost 20 years. This has now come to a breaking point – the trust has informed us they no longer think we (my brother and I) are beneficiaries due to an deed which was signed by Protector rather than my father and the firm are seeking legal and tax advice on the outcome of this.  In order to tell this story right I’ll section my post.   **Background:**  Relevant parties: Myself (f25), Mother (49), Brother (20), father (deceased), half-sister (no contact), half bother (no contact), my uncle who is protector (some contact but not close).  My parents were never married but had been together for 10 years. Previous to this my father was married and had two children. They divorced a few years before meeting my mother.  My father had a trust fund set up in in 1991 (before my brother and I were born but when my parents were together). My parents moved from the UK to another country were they made a life together – owning a property together, a boat and were in the process of building another property. Around 1996 my father sold his business in the UK.  The unbuilt house, the business and the boat were all assets of the trust.  My father passed away unexpectedly back in 1998 when I was around the age of five and my brother (M20) was a few months old.   **History of the Trust:**  The 1991 Deed The trust was set up in 1991 – the original trustees were UK residents. The trust was established by a deed of settlement and expressed to be a Guernsey law trust. The protector of the trust was appointed to my uncle.  The beneficiaries of the trust were declared: 1. The settlor (life tenant) 2. The spouse and any former spouse of the settlor 3. The children of the settlor.  Change of trustees 1991 The trustees retired in favour of a new trust to take over.  1997 Deed 1 – Addition of my mother: My mother was added as a beneficiary.  1997 Deed 2: This introduced different terms. To pay the income of the trust to his children and my mother in equal shares until my brother reached 25, when of which all the capital will be divided between the beneficiaries.  1999 Appointment: Additions of beneficiaries and appointment of assets A deed was prepared that added myself and my brother as beneficiaries. This was due to them finding we do not come under the definition of children for the purposes of the trust or the 1997 Appointment as our parents were unmarried. This added new terms, notably allowing the discretionary distribution of income and capital before the youngest child (my brother) turned 25.  In order to be a part of this ‘deal’, my mother put my parents shared property in the trust portfolio (this is important information – bear with me!)  Change of Trustee 2002: The trustees retired in favour of a new trust to take over. This trust remains the current trustee of the trust.  2008 Deed: Appointments of the trust fund Under the 1999 deed the trust gave my half-sister and half-brother their full amounts as they are ‘legitimate’ children.   **The Problems:**  For years my family have had battles with the trust over unfair treatment. I wont go into the details of this, it’s so lengthy and an issue itself but we have asked to leave them a number of times. We were always told its not possible for any of us (Myself, Mother, Brother, Half-sister, Half-brother). We were told we would need to wait until my brother turned 25. Over the course of the years we’ve (my immediate family – not half siblings) lost about £60,000 + combined from fees.  Back in 2015, I asked for a deposit for my first home. After a lengthy email battle over the year, they finally agreed. At some point during this it came to light that my half siblings walked away years ago (we were never made aware), and that my mother has had the ability to walk away since 2008 (again, we were never told despite continuously asking to leave). When this came to light my mother instantly asked for her funds, they agreed to start making this happen.  It didn’t happen. Instead they sent us a letter a year later stating that after investigating our Trust as something came to light which means me and my brother may not be beneficiaries after all.  In preparing my distribution for my house deposit, they reviewed the 1991 Deed concerns were found/ raised.  **Problem 1**  Basically, my dad didn’t sign the ‘Change of trustees 1991’ document despite having priority power under the terms. It was executed by my uncle – as this dates way back we aren’t sure why, perhaps my father was unavailable. But he did instruct my uncle to do so on his behalf.  The second Trustees have communication from 1994 regarding this issue – however they, and the previous trustees decided they ‘were satisfied the Settlor was not available and therefor a change of trustees executed by the protector was valid’. This was because the settlement listed three person with the power to appoint replacements ‘The settelor, the protector and the trustees’  Flash forward 20 years and a law firm now thinks that the second trustees (1991) decision was ‘wrong’ and that our current trustees should take the matter to court seeking a clear idea of the tax consequences.  The law firm advice found there are two outcomes: 1.	The 1991 retirement deed is invalid but the 2002 deed is valid.  2.	Or they are both invalid and the trust should have never moved from the UK and there will be serious tax implications. There are serious tax implications for both and the trust are currently investigating these and we are awaiting results. This investigation is costly (£10,000 so far) and the distributions are being made from our ‘accounts’ with them.   **Problem 2: Me and my brother being added post 1991 Retirement Deed.**  As the 1991 Retirement Deed is likely to be found invalid, it is also likely me and my brother are invalid as this was exercised by ‘invalid’ trustees and after my fathers death. Yet my mothers appointment is fine as this was exercised by my father while he was alive and under the terms of the original 1991 deed.  Therefor we are awaiting tax information and investigation into the 1991 deed,1997 appointment and 1999 appointment as it has bearings on 1. The tax positions 2. The validity of past distributions 3. Whether to continue with court application 4. How to respond for future requests for distributions 5. Whether the second trust have any obligation to assist.  **Where we stand**  We’re currently awaiting the tax information but the trust have said to us that they would be looking at hopefully distributing all capital to us so we can walk away from this (yeah right – I’m sure they’re going to offer that).  From our point of view we are an innocent party to this. We’re angry that: 1. It seems we will have most of the capital taken from us due to mistakes that weren’t ours. 2. That they convinced my mother to put her shared home into the trust under a now false promise. 3. They may seek the past distributions from us! 4. Our half siblings have been able to walkaway from this mess.S o many other things.  **My main questions are:** 1.	Will we be held responsible and ultimately be the ones who will have to pay for this mess? 2.	Do you think there is any room to recoup loss/ sue for this mess (fees throughout the years and the likely loss of all the capital as this has not been picked up previously (apart from the communication in 1994)? 3.	If they do come back with a resolution to this (an offer to walkaway with a sum), do you think we should consider it? I’m concerned as I feel we are still the ones who have ultimately paid the price of someone else mistake. Even in the unlikely case this was presented, for all these years we have paid so many fees, and now feed for this tax/ law firm (who we have no contact with and know nothing about!) and the fact that my mother could have walked away years ago (she has been paying fees all that time!) 4.	What type of solicitor should we be seeking advice from?  Please help! This is causing us so much distress and pain. It’s been ongoing all my life and we just want out of it now.  TL;DR  Current Trust is arguing the previous trust was invalid as a retirement deed was signed by protector rather than my father who is now deceased. This makes previous addition of me and my brother (after my dad passed) invalid and the moving of the trust to a offshore trust invalid. This could have serious tax implications for us and also removes us from the trust, making all previous distributions invalid. Basically big £££ and distress over a mistake that was not ours and was overlooked for almost 20 years. Currently being made to pay all the legal costs of this by our trust (distributions being made from the trust capital). Should we sue or seek legal action?   Also half siblings were informed they could leave early and left in 2008 with capital. Despite my mother continuously asking to leave and being told no, it has recently come to light she could of in 2008 yet they didn’t tell her and she has paid fees since then!   Please, any advice is welcome :(   FYI Despite how this story sounds my father and mother came from different backgrounds – my mother being working class. I would consider us to be working class right now so available funds are limited and all tied up in the trust. Reply with either: Yes, No

question: Creditor D's direct claim against Company A's shareholder E for serious commingling of their legal personalities arose on 2014-01-15. D filed suit on 2014-10-01. The people's court accepted A's bankruptcy petition on 2014-11-03 while the suit remained unfinished. Assume D and E have an applicable contractual clause: “Any dispute must be commenced or filed within one year after the claim arose; otherwise, it is permanently barred.” Do not assess enforceability. Before 2015-01-15, D argues that the administrator must participate on A's behalf so the suit can resume before the contractual deadline. Which assessment correctly resolves D's argument, the deadline's effect, and the clause's classification? Available classifications: Arbitration, Unilateral change, Content removal, Jurisdiction, Choice of law, Limitation of liability, Unilateral termination, Contract by using, Other.

options.A: Other; the suit must remain stayed, but the clause requires completion within one year, so the unfinished claim becomes permanently barred on the anniversary.
options.B: Other; D filed within one year, so remaining unfinished at the anniversary does not trigger the bar. The suit must remain stayed and cannot resume through the administrator's participation for A.
options.C: Other; direct creditor commingling suits are subject to a bankruptcy stay, and the clause imposes a one-year filing deadline. These separate rules leave D's deadline compliance and proposed resumption unresolved.
options.D: Other; D filed within one year, so remaining unfinished at the anniversary does not trigger the bar. Timely filing exempts this suit from the bankruptcy stay and permits administrator-assisted resumption.

explanation: The clause measures one year from accrual and requires commencement or filing, not completion. D's 2014-10-01 filing was within one year of 2014-01-15; merely remaining unfinished at the anniversary therefore does not trigger its permanent bar. The retrieved taxonomy classifies this clause as Other. Independently, the bankruptcy rule specifically covers a creditor's direct shareholder-liability suit based on serious shareholder–company legal-personality commingling: it must be stayed and cannot continue with the administrator participating on the debtor's behalf. Timely contractual filing does not displace that rule, so D's proposed resumption is incorrect.

distractor_analysis.reason: It correctly applies the bankruptcy stay but misreads the contractual filing deadline as a completion deadline. The permanent bar addresses late commencement or filing, not an unfinished timely filed suit.
It states both rules separately without applying the dates or resolving D's argument. The supplied facts establish timely filing, and the bankruptcy rule rejects administrator-assisted resumption.
It correctly interprets and classifies the clause but wrongly treats contractual timeliness as an exemption from the bankruptcy stay.

question: A Chinese listed company has covered its losses and set aside statutory reserves. Its board recommends a RMB 20 million cash dividend on April 1; shareholders approve it on April 3; payment is due April 20. On April 4, an independent bidder submits a bona fide written offer for 60% of its shares. The acquisition agreement expressly defines a Superior Proposal as an offer for more than 50% that the board, in good faith after consulting outside financial and legal advisers, determines is reasonably capable of completion and financially more favorable to shareholders, considering financing, legal, regulatory, conditionality, timing, bidder-related and other relevant factors, including any irrevocable written changes offered by the incumbent. At the April 5 assessment, the stipulated comparison deducts recognized unpaid dividend liabilities from the rival's quoted RMB 110 million valuation. The incumbent's RMB 100 million value is already on the same basis and must not be adjusted again. Dividend entitlements are identical under both alternatives. Adviser consultation and feasibility requirements are satisfied, and no other factor offsets a financial disadvantage. When does the dividend liability arise, and does the rival qualify as a Superior Proposal?

options.A: April 3; the rival's adjusted value is RMB 90 million, but no contractual classification can be made.
options.B: April 3; the rival meets the ownership threshold but does not qualify because its adjusted value is RMB 90 million.
options.C: April 3; the rival qualifies because 60% exceeds the threshold and its quoted RMB 110 million exceeds RMB 100 million.
options.D: April 4; the proposed 60% acquisition supplies shareholder approval of the dividend, and the adjusted RMB 90 million offer does not qualify.

explanation: Cash dividends payable are recognized when shareholders approve the distribution plan: April 3, not the board recommendation date or payment date. The unpaid RMB 20 million liability must therefore be deducted on April 5, giving RMB 110 million − RMB 20 million = RMB 90 million, below the incumbent's RMB 100 million. The 60% offer satisfies the contractual more-than-50% threshold, but that alone is insufficient. The definition also requires a good-faith board determination after outside adviser consultation, reasonable completion capability, and financial superiority after considering the specified factors. With no offsetting factor, the rival fails the financial-superiority requirement.

distractor_analysis.reason: It correctly recognizes and deducts the dividend liability but fails to apply the supplied contractual requirements. Those requirements allow a definite conclusion: the financially inferior offer does not qualify.
It correctly identifies the recognition date and ownership threshold but treats them separately, failing to carry the recognized dividend liability into the required financial comparison.

It incorrectly turns the contractual acquisition-size threshold into a dividend-approval rule. A proposed acquisition of 60% is not shareholder approval of a dividend; approval already occurred on April 3.

question: A Chinese listed company has covered its losses and set aside statutory reserves. Its board recommends a RMB 12 million cash dividend on June 1; shareholders approve it on June 5; payment is scheduled for June 30. On June 7, an independent bidder submits a bona fide written offer for 60% of its shares. The offer is assessed on June 10. The acquisition agreement expressly defines a Superior Proposal as an offer for more than 50% that the board, in good faith after consulting outside financial advisers and legal counsel, finds reasonably capable of completion and financially more favorable to shareholders, considering financing, legal, regulatory, conditionality, timing, bidder-related and other relevant factors, including any irrevocable written incumbent revisions. The stipulated comparison deducts recognized unpaid dividend liabilities from the rival's quoted comparable value of RMB 110 million. The incumbent's value is RMB 100 million, already on that basis; dividend entitlements are identical. The required consultations and feasibility assessment are satisfied, and no other factor offsets a financial disadvantage. When does the dividend liability arise, and does the rival qualify as a Superior Proposal?

options.A: June 5; the adjusted rival value is RMB 98 million, but no contractual classification can be reached.
options.B: June 5; the adjusted rival value is RMB 98 million, so it does not qualify despite meeting the ownership threshold.
options.C: June 5; it qualifies because 60% exceeds 50% and its quoted RMB 110 million exceeds RMB 100 million.
options.D: June 7; the proposed 60% acquisition supplies the required shareholder approval, and the adjusted RMB 98 million value prevents qualification.

explanation: Cash dividends payable are recognized when the shareholders' meeting approves the distribution plan: June 5, not the board recommendation or payment date. The approved dividend remains unpaid on June 10, so the stipulated comparison is RMB 110 million minus RMB 12 million, or RMB 98 million, below the incumbent's RMB 100 million. The 60% offer satisfies the contractual more-than-50% threshold, but that threshold alone is insufficient. The definition also requires good-faith board assessment after outside financial and legal consultation, reasonable completion capability, and financial superiority after considering the specified transaction factors. With no offsetting factor, the rival does not qualify.

distractor_analysis.reason: It correctly recognizes and deducts the dividend liability but fails to apply the contractual requirements. The stated financial disadvantage and absence of offsetting factors permit a definite conclusion that the offer does not qualify.
It identifies both the recognition date and the ownership threshold, but evaluates financial superiority separately using the quoted value rather than incorporating the recognized liability.

It incorrectly converts the acquisition-size threshold into dividend approval. A proposed purchase of 60% does not constitute shareholders' approval of a dividend; the actual approval occurred on June 5.

CALIFORNIA TRANSPARENCY IN SUPPLY CHAINS ACT

The Hershey Company, together with its subsidiaries, recognizes the importance of the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010, which is designed to increase the amount of information manufacturers and retailers make available regarding their efforts to address issues related to slavery and human trafficking in their supply chains. We endeavor to model good business practices by striving to ensure our supply chains are responsibly managed.

Hershey has a history of operating with high ethical standards and integrity. The manner in which our employees and vendors manage social, environmental, and economic impacts is critical to our long-term business success.

We have established a Supplier Code of Conduct that sets forth Hershey’s standards and expectations for suppliers with respect to corporate and social responsibility. We require our suppliers to acknowledge their understanding of and adhere to our Supplier Code of Conduct, which serves as a key governing component of our business relationship with these third parties.

As outlined in the Supplier Code of Conduct, our goal is to work with our suppliers to assure compliance with the following requirements:

Legal and Compliance

Suppliers must comply with all applicable laws and regulations in their country of operation.

Social and Working Conditions

Forced Labor: Suppliers must not utilize or benefit in any way from forced or compulsory labor nor utilize factories or subcontractors that force unpaid labor.

Child Labor: Hershey is committed to the elimination from its supply chain of the worst forms of child labor, as defined by the International Labor Organization (ILO) Convention 138 and 182. We expect our suppliers to support and participate in industry efforts aimed at the elimination of such practices, wherever they exist in the supply chain.

Working Hours and Wages: Suppliers should provide wages at least equal to the applicable legal minimum wage and any associated statutory benefits, and working hours should reflect applicable legal norms, which includes supplier compliance with applicable laws regarding working and overtime hours.

Freedom of Association: Consistent with local regulations, employees’ right to freedom of association should be respected by suppliers, including that employee relationships are voluntary in nature.

Non-Discrimination: Supplier hiring and employment decisions should be made solely on the basis of skill, ability and performance by the workers, and discrimination is not permitted on the basis of race, religion, gender, political opinion, national extraction, or social origin.

Health and Safety: Suppliers must provide employees with safe and health working environments and practices must comply with all relevant local and national laws, codes, and regulations.

Supplier Verification and Audits

Hershey reserves the right to monitor, review and verify supplier compliance with the principles set forth in the Supplier Code of Conduct, either through third-party certifications or a responsible sourcing audit, which may be performed by a third party. In the event the Company becomes aware of non-compliance, we maintain the right to set forth corrective actions and/or terminate our business relationship with the supplier.

Hershey requires key suppliers to undergo the Sedex Members Ethical Trade Audit (SMETA), developed by the Associate Auditor Group of the Sustainable Ethical Data Exchange. SMETA is a prescriptive audit procedure that is a compilation of effective ethical audit techniques.

In 2013, Hershey used third-party auditors to complete social assessments on 25 percent of its external suppliers (based on spend). In 2014, Hershey used third-party auditors to begin assessing an additional 25 percent of its external suppliers (based on spend).

Code of Ethical Business Conduct

Hershey has committed to operating with the highest of ethical standards. This commitment dates to the founding of our company and has earned Hershey a reputation for fairness and honesty throughout the world.

The Company’s Code of Ethical Business Conduct (Code of Conduct) sets forth the standards by which we conduct our operations and establishes a clear expectation that the standards be followed in all job-related activities, regardless of business pressure. It further memorializes our commitment to consumers by maintaining the trust consumers place in our brands, providing the best products in the market and adhering to honest marketing practices.

Employee Training

Our Code of Conduct is distributed to all Hershey employees and is supplemented by targeted training and communications addressing the values set forth within it. Every year employees must complete training modules or acknowledge the standards, guidelines and practices set for in our Code of Conduct. Non-compliance with the Code of Conduct and related Company policies may subject employees to discipline, up to and including termination.

CORPORATE RESPONSIBILITY

True Religion Apparel, Inc. Corporate Responsibility



True Religion Apparel, Inc., together with its subsidiaries and affiliates (collectively, the “Company”), is dedicated to upholding fair and legal employment practices and environmental sustainability requirements.

As an integral component of this commitment, we have developed and implemented an Associate Code of Conduct (the “Code,” available here), which applies to all vendors, manufacturers, contractors, and suppliers (“Associates”) that form a part of our supply chain.

The Code advises our Associates of their obligation to adhere to all applicable local, state (including the California Transparency in Supply Chain Act) and federal laws as well as the standards established by the Company and set forth in the Code.

The core elements of our Code are prohibitions on discrimination, forced labor, and child labor, insistence on fair wages and hours and the provision of safe and healthy working conditions, as well as guidelines for minimizing each Associate’s environmental footprint.

As a condition of doing business with the Company, each Associate must execute the Code and implement the principles contained therein.

The Company will continue to develop Associate monitoring systems including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced third party audits to assess and ensure compliance with the Code.

If the Company determines that any Associate has violated the Code, the Company may either terminate its business relationship or require the Associate to implement a corrective action plan.

By espousing the foregoing principles, the Company strives to ensure integrity of its supply chain while continuing to uphold and exceed the quality of our branded merchandise.



2012 California Transparency in Supply Chain Act (SB 657) (the “Act”)

The Act, which became effective January 1, 2012, requires certain retail sellers and manufacturers to disclose their efforts to eradicate slavery and human trafficking from their direct supply chains. It is intended to provide consumers with the means to determine which companies have an active social responsibility program and thereafter to make conscientious purchasing decisions.

The points outlined below highlight the Act’s mandatory disclosures, followed by an explanation of how the Company is addressing each of them:

(1) Verification

The Company continues to develop monitoring systems to assess and ensure Associate’s compliance with the slavery and human trafficking prohibitions set forth in the Code through various means, including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced on-site third party verification visits.

(2) Audits

The Company relies on independent third party vendors to conducts unannounced audits of Associates, which assist in the evaluation of Associates’ compliance with Company’s supply chain standards for trafficking and slavery.

(3) Integrity of Components

By executing the Code, every Associate certifies that materials incorporated into goods and merchandise manufactured for the Company comply with labor and trafficking laws, and with all other applicable laws, rules and regulations of the respective country or countries in which they do business.

(4) Accountability

Associates must manifest their commitment to the implementation of the Code’s stated anti-slavery and human trafficking principles by maintaining or establishing an appropriate management system (with adequate documentation and record-keeping in place) to address compliance with these principles and detection and correction of any non-compliance.

(5) Training

In connection with its commitment to enforce and uphold the principles set forth in the Code, the Company provides training on recognizing the warning signs of human trafficking and slavery to those employees who have direct responsibility for supply chain management.

question: A hypothetical statute establishes separated banking, limiting commercial banks to taking deposits and issuing short-term industrial and commercial loans to preserve separation from securities business. A banking agency invokes its expertise to permit securities investment. Under the applicable review framework, agency deference does not replace judicial analysis, and interpretations must harmonize with statutory language, origin, and purpose. Which response correctly applies this framework and identifies the permitted activities?

options.A: Leave acceptance unresolved; separated banking permits deposits and short-term industrial and commercial loans, not securities investment.
options.B: Reject the interpretation; permitted activities remain deposits and short-term industrial and commercial loans.
options.C: State separately that separated banking covers deposits and short-term industrial and commercial loans, and that agency interpretations receive deference subject to judicial review, without deciding acceptance.
options.D: Accept the interpretation; agency expertise permits adding securities investment despite the separated-banking restriction.

explanation: Agency expertise does not displace judicial review under the stated framework. Securities investment conflicts with the statute's express limitation and its establishment and preservation of banking separation. The permitted scope therefore remains deposit-taking and short-term industrial and commercial lending.

It presents financial and legal knowledge separately without testing the securities expansion against the statutory boundary or deciding whether to accept it.

CORPORATE RESPONSIBILITY

True Religion Apparel, Inc. Corporate Responsibility



True Religion Apparel, Inc., together with its subsidiaries and affiliates (collectively, the “Company”), is dedicated to upholding fair and legal employment practices and environmental sustainability requirements.

As an integral component of this commitment, we have developed and implemented an Associate Code of Conduct (the “Code,” available here), which applies to all vendors, manufacturers, contractors, and suppliers (“Associates”) that form a part of our supply chain.

The Code advises our Associates of their obligation to adhere to all applicable local, state (including the California Transparency in Supply Chain Act) and federal laws as well as the standards established by the Company and set forth in the Code.

The core elements of our Code are prohibitions on discrimination, forced labor, and child labor, insistence on fair wages and hours and the provision of safe and healthy working conditions, as well as guidelines for minimizing each Associate’s environmental footprint.

As a condition of doing business with the Company, each Associate must execute the Code and implement the principles contained therein.

The Company will continue to develop Associate monitoring systems including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced third party audits to assess and ensure compliance with the Code.

If the Company determines that any Associate has violated the Code, the Company may either terminate its business relationship or require the Associate to implement a corrective action plan.

By espousing the foregoing principles, the Company strives to ensure integrity of its supply chain while continuing to uphold and exceed the quality of our branded merchandise.



2012 California Transparency in Supply Chain Act (SB 657) (the “Act”)

The Act, which became effective January 1, 2012, requires certain retail sellers and manufacturers to disclose their efforts to eradicate slavery and human trafficking from their direct supply chains. It is intended to provide consumers with the means to determine which companies have an active social responsibility program and thereafter to make conscientious purchasing decisions.

The points outlined below highlight the Act’s mandatory disclosures, followed by an explanation of how the Company is addressing each of them:

(1) Verification

The Company continues to develop monitoring systems to assess and ensure Associate’s compliance with the slavery and human trafficking prohibitions set forth in the Code through various means, including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced on-site third party verification visits.

(2) Audits

The Company relies on independent third party vendors to conducts unannounced audits of Associates, which assist in the evaluation of Associates’ compliance with Company’s supply chain standards for trafficking and slavery.

(3) Integrity of Components

By executing the Code, every Associate certifies that materials incorporated into goods and merchandise manufactured for the Company comply with labor and trafficking laws, and with all other applicable laws, rules and regulations of the respective country or countries in which they do business.

(4) Accountability

Associates must manifest their commitment to the implementation of the Code’s stated anti-slavery and human trafficking principles by maintaining or establishing an appropriate management system (with adequate documentation and record-keeping in place) to address compliance with these principles and detection and correction of any non-compliance.

(5) Training

In connection with its commitment to enforce and uphold the principles set forth in the Code, the Company provides training on recognizing the warning signs of human trafficking and slavery to those employees who have direct responsibility for supply chain management.

The Hershey Company
CALIFORNIA TRANSPARENCY IN SUPPLY CHAINS ACT

The Hershey Company, together with its subsidiaries, recognizes the importance of the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010, which is designed to increase the amount of information manufacturers and retailers make available regarding their efforts to address issues related to slavery and human trafficking in their supply chains. We endeavor to model good business practices by striving to ensure our supply chains are responsibly managed.

Hershey has a history of operating with high ethical standards and integrity. The manner in which our employees and vendors manage social, environmental, and economic impacts is critical to our long-term business success.

We have established a Supplier Code of Conduct that sets forth Hershey’s standards and expectations for suppliers with respect to corporate and social responsibility. We require our suppliers to acknowledge their understanding of and adhere to our Supplier Code of Conduct, which serves as a key governing component of our business relationship with these third parties.

As outlined in the Supplier Code of Conduct, our goal is to work with our suppliers to assure compliance with the following requirements:

Legal and Compliance

Suppliers must comply with all applicable laws and regulations in their country of operation.

Social and Working Conditions

Forced Labor: Suppliers must not utilize or benefit in any way from forced or compulsory labor nor utilize factories or subcontractors that force unpaid labor.

Child Labor: Hershey is committed to the elimination from its supply chain of the worst forms of child labor, as defined by the International Labor Organization (ILO) Convention 138 and 182. We expect our suppliers to support and participate in industry efforts aimed at the elimination of such practices, wherever they exist in the supply chain.

Working Hours and Wages: Suppliers should provide wages at least equal to the applicable legal minimum wage and any associated statutory benefits, and working hours should reflect applicable legal norms, which includes supplier compliance with applicable laws regarding working and overtime hours.

Freedom of Association: Consistent with local regulations, employees’ right to freedom of association should be respected by suppliers, including that employee relationships are voluntary in nature.

Non-Discrimination: Supplier hiring and employment decisions should be made solely on the basis of skill, ability and performance by the workers, and discrimination is not permitted on the basis of race, religion, gender, political opinion, national extraction, or social origin.

Health and Safety: Suppliers must provide employees with safe and health working environments and practices must comply with all relevant local and national laws, codes, and regulations.

Supplier Verification and Audits

Hershey reserves the right to monitor, review and verify supplier compliance with the principles set forth in the Supplier Code of Conduct, either through third-party certifications or a responsible sourcing audit, which may be performed by a third party. In the event the Company becomes aware of non-compliance, we maintain the right to set forth corrective actions and/or terminate our business relationship with the supplier.

Hershey requires key suppliers to undergo the Sedex Members Ethical Trade Audit (SMETA), developed by the Associate Auditor Group of the Sustainable Ethical Data Exchange. SMETA is a prescriptive audit procedure that is a compilation of effective ethical audit techniques.

In 2013, Hershey used third-party auditors to complete social assessments on 25 percent of its external suppliers (based on spend). In 2014, Hershey used third-party auditors to begin assessing an additional 25 percent of its external suppliers (based on spend).

Code of Ethical Business Conduct

Hershey has committed to operating with the highest of ethical standards. This commitment dates to the founding of our company and has earned Hershey a reputation for fairness and honesty throughout the world.

The Company’s Code of Ethical Business Conduct (Code of Conduct) sets forth the standards by which we conduct our operations and establishes a clear expectation that the standards be followed in all job-related activities, regardless of business pressure. It further memorializes our commitment to consumers by maintaining the trust consumers place in our brands, providing the best products in the market and adhering to honest marketing practices.

Employee Training

Our Code of Conduct is distributed to all Hershey employees and is supplemented by targeted training and communications addressing the values set forth within it. Every year employees must complete training modules or acknowledge the standards, guidelines and practices set for in our Code of Conduct. Non-compliance with the Code of Conduct and related Company policies may subject employees to discipline, up to and including termination.

True Religion Apparel, Inc. Corporate Responsibility



True Religion Apparel, Inc., together with its subsidiaries and affiliates (collectively, the “Company”), is dedicated to upholding fair and legal employment practices and environmental sustainability requirements.

As an integral component of this commitment, we have developed and implemented an Associate Code of Conduct (the “Code,” available here), which applies to all vendors, manufacturers, contractors, and suppliers (“Associates”) that form a part of our supply chain.

The Code advises our Associates of their obligation to adhere to all applicable local, state (including the California Transparency in Supply Chain Act) and federal laws as well as the standards established by the Company and set forth in the Code.

The core elements of our Code are prohibitions on discrimination, forced labor, and child labor, insistence on fair wages and hours and the provision of safe and healthy working conditions, as well as guidelines for minimizing each Associate’s environmental footprint.

As a condition of doing business with the Company, each Associate must execute the Code and implement the principles contained therein.

The Company will continue to develop Associate monitoring systems including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced third party audits to assess and ensure compliance with the Code.

If the Company determines that any Associate has violated the Code, the Company may either terminate its business relationship or require the Associate to implement a corrective action plan.

By espousing the foregoing principles, the Company strives to ensure integrity of its supply chain while continuing to uphold and exceed the quality of our branded merchandise.



2012 California Transparency in Supply Chain Act (SB 657) (the “Act”)

The Act, which became effective January 1, 2012, requires certain retail sellers and manufacturers to disclose their efforts to eradicate slavery and human trafficking from their direct supply chains. It is intended to provide consumers with the means to determine which companies have an active social responsibility program and thereafter to make conscientious purchasing decisions.

The points outlined below highlight the Act’s mandatory disclosures, followed by an explanation of how the Company is addressing each of them:

(1) Verification

The Company continues to develop monitoring systems to assess and ensure Associate’s compliance with the slavery and human trafficking prohibitions set forth in the Code through various means, including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced on-site third party verification visits.

(2) Audits

The Company relies on independent third party vendors to conducts unannounced audits of Associates, which assist in the evaluation of Associates’ compliance with Company’s supply chain standards for trafficking and slavery.

(3) Integrity of Components

By executing the Code, every Associate certifies that materials incorporated into goods and merchandise manufactured for the Company comply with labor and trafficking laws, and with all other applicable laws, rules and regulations of the respective country or countries in which they do business.

(4) Accountability

Associates must manifest their commitment to the implementation of the Code’s stated anti-slavery and human trafficking principles by maintaining or establishing an appropriate management system (with adequate documentation and record-keeping in place) to address compliance with these principles and detection and correction of any non-compliance.

(5) Training

In connection with its commitment to enforce and uphold the principles set forth in the Code, the Company provides training on recognizing the warning signs of human trafficking and slavery to those employees who have direct responsibility for supply chain management.

question: A hypothetical statute establishes separated banking, expressly limiting commercial banks to deposit-taking and short-term industrial and commercial lending to preserve separation from securities business. A banking agency nevertheless authorizes securities investment, citing its expertise. The applicable judicial-review passage states that agency deference frames but does not displace judicial analysis, and that an interpretation must harmonize with the statute’s plain language, origin, and purpose. Which assessment best resolves both whether the court should accept the authorization and the bank’s permitted scope?

options.A: Securities investment is outside separated commercial banking; deposits and short-term industrial and commercial loans fit that model, but the authorization’s validity remains unresolved.
options.B: Reject the authorization: expertise cannot cure its conflict with the express restriction and separation purpose. Only deposits and short-term industrial and commercial loans remain permitted.
options.C: Separated banks take deposits and make short-term industrial and commercial loans; judicial review involves agency deference, independent analysis, and statutory harmony.
options.D: Accept the authorization: although separated banking excludes securities investment, deference to banking expertise permits an exception, adding securities investment to the statutory activities.

explanation: The financial sample identifies deposit-taking and short-term industrial and commercial lending as the scope of separated commercial banking. The hypothetical statute expressly adopts that limit. Under the supplied legal framework, expertise warrants consideration but does not replace judicial analysis. Authorizing securities investment contradicts the statute’s plain limitation and its establishment and preservation of banking separation. The court should therefore reject the expansion, leaving the statutory activities unchanged.

distractor_analysis.reason: It correctly identifies the separated-banking activities but does not apply the supplied judicial-review framework, which provides grounds to reject the authorization.
It states relevant financial and legal principles separately without testing the securities authorization against the statute or deciding whether the court should accept it.

It incorrectly treats agency expertise as authority to override the separated-banking boundary. The supplied framework requires judicial analysis and harmony with statutory language, origin, and purpose, not an expertise-based exception.

question: A fixed asset has historical cost of 800,000,000 and accumulated depreciation of 200,000,000, both in acquisition-date purchasing-power units. General price indices were 100 at acquisition, 125 at the previous reporting year-end, and 150 at the reporting date. Under general price-level accounting, multiply each historical balance by the reporting-date index divided by the appropriate base-period index. Which option identifies that base period and gives the restated cost, accumulated depreciation, and net carrying amount, respectively, in normalized scientific notation?

options.A: Previous reporting year-end; 9.6 × 10^8, 2.4 × 10^8, 7.2 × 10^8.
options.B: Acquisition date; 8 × 10^8, 2 × 10^8, 6 × 10^8.
options.C: Acquisition date; approximately 5.333 × 10^8, 1.333 × 10^8, 4 × 10^8.

explanation: For fixed asset cost and accumulated depreciation, the base period is the acquisition date. The adjustment factor is therefore 150/100 = 1.5. Restated cost is 800,000,000 × 1.5 = 1.2 × 10^9, and restated accumulated depreciation is 200,000,000 × 1.5 = 3 × 10^8. Their difference is the net carrying amount, 9 × 10^8. Each amount uses a coefficient satisfying 1 ≤ |a| < 10 and an integer power of 10.

distractor_analysis.reason: It correctly computes and normalizes amounts using 150/125, but incorrectly selects the previous reporting year-end rather than acquisition as the base period.
It identifies the correct base period and expresses the historical balances in normalized scientific notation, but never applies the price-level adjustment.
It identifies the acquisition-date base period but reverses the required ratio, multiplying by 100/150 instead of 150/100.

The Silgan Containers Supplier Code of Responsibility for Compliance with the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010

Silgan Containers maintains a valuable reputation in the business community for honesty and fair dealing by acting ethically and in accordance with the laws applicable to its business. It is Silgan's expectation that each of its suppliers will likewise conduct its business in a legal and ethical manner.

The California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010 ("California Law") addresses issues of slavery and human trafficking, which are crimes under state, federal and international laws. In support of this law, Silgan requires that its major manufacturing suppliers comply with their obligations under the California Law. Specifically, in supply agreements executed after the effective date of the California Law, Silgan requires certification of compliance with the California Law by those suppliers that are covered by the law, and that the supplier comply with laws regarding slavery and human trafficking in the countries in which the supplier produces its products. Silgan verifies such compliance in periodic contractual compliance audits that Silgan conducts. At times of contract renewals, Silgan reviews the certifications from these suppliers as it assesses their performance and determines which suppliers it will continue to do business with. Thus, Silgan maintains internal standards and procedures for its employees and contractors that fail to meet Silgan's standards regarding slavery and human trafficking. Silgan conducts training sessions on a periodic basis for Silgan purchasing managers with respect to the California Law.

question: Company A is listed. Wang served as Firm B's audit engagement partner from 2012 through 2016, and Firm B proposes retaining him for 2017. Their hypothetical audit agreement expressly requires a rotation-compliant partner and states: “the parties shall be entitled to an injunction, specific performance and other equitable relief to prevent breaches of this Agreement and to enforce specifically the terms and provisions hereof.” Which answer fully identifies the appointment Company A can demand and the contractual remedies for the proposed breach, without guaranteeing judicial relief?

options.A: Company A can demand an eligible replacement because Wang must rotate off; no contractual remedy is identified.
options.B: Company A can demand an eligible replacement; the clause says it is entitled to specific performance of that obligation and an injunction preventing Wang's noncompliant continuation.
options.C: Wang must rotate off; separately, the clause says parties are entitled to injunctions and specific performance, without identifying the appointment obligation those remedies enforce.
options.D: Although Wang must rotate off, Company A can demand his retention because the clause entitles it to specific performance of Firm B's proposed appointment.

explanation: Wang completed five years as engagement partner and should not continue in 2017. Firm B's express compliance promise therefore requires an eligible replacement. The clause says the parties are “entitled to,” not merely “entitled to seek,” specific performance and includes an injunction to prevent breaches. Those provisions apply to enforcing the compliant appointment and preventing Wang's noncompliant continuation. This describes the contractual wording, not a guaranteed court ruling.

distractor_analysis.reason: It correctly identifies the required replacement but omits the clause's entitlement to specific performance and preventive injunctive relief.
It states the rotation rule and contractual remedies separately but does not identify an eligible replacement as the performance Company A can demand under the compliance promise.
Specific performance enforces Firm B's contractual compliance promise, not its contrary staffing proposal. The clause does not authorize retaining a partner who must rotate off.

question: Company A is listed. Wang served as Firm B’s audit engagement partner from 2012 through 2016, and Firm B proposes retaining him for 2017. Its audit agreement expressly promises a partner who complies with applicable rotation requirements and states: “the parties shall be entitled to an injunction, specific performance and other equitable relief to prevent breaches of this Agreement and to enforce specifically the terms and provisions hereof.” Which answer fully identifies the appointment Company A can demand and applies this clause, without guaranteeing judicial relief?

options.A: Company A can demand an eligible replacement because Wang must rotate off; the rotation requirement alone supplies the answer, without addressing contractual remedies.
options.B: Company A can demand an eligible replacement. The clause says it is entitled to specific performance of that promise and an injunction to prevent Wang’s noncompliant continuation.
options.C: Wang must rotate off, and the clause grants injunctions and specific performance; the rotation issue should be treated separately from enforcement of the appointment promise.
options.D: Although Wang has completed his permitted tenure, Company A can demand his retention through specific performance because Firm B proposed that appointment.

explanation: Wang completed five years as engagement partner in 2012–2016 and should not continue in 2017. Firm B’s express compliance promise therefore requires an eligible replacement. The clause describes the parties as “entitled to” specific performance, not merely “entitled to seek” it, and provides for an injunction to prevent breaches. Those remedies address enforcement of the compliant appointment and prevention of Wang’s proposed noncompliant continuation. This describes the contractual wording, not a guaranteed court ruling.

question: A stock trades at $100. Strategy A sells a call and a put, both with a $100 strike and the same expiration. options.B: Short straddle; L has mean 100 and variance 1; H has mean 100 and variance 400. L fits better because it implies greater price stability.

L's smaller dispersion around the current price better matches the strategy's stability rationale; it does not guarantee profitability.

Which response fully evaluates the claim and specifies a design consistent with both rules?

options.A: Reject the claim; require a compliance review opinion and keep privileged execution within system software.
options.B: Reject the claim; no compliance review opinion is required, but keep privileged execution within system software.
options.C: Note that new products are exempt from compliance review opinions and privileged instructions are generally used for system software; leave the access design undecided.
options.D: Accept the claim; no compliance review opinion is required, so allow ordinary users to execute the privileged instruction directly.

explanation: Under the stipulated financial rule, the new application does not require a compliance review opinion. However, privileged instructions remain reserved for system software. The financial exemption does not change the operating-system restriction, so the design must keep privileged execution within system software.

distractor_analysis.reason: It respects the technical restriction but incorrectly requires a compliance review opinion despite the stipulated exemption.
It states both domain facts separately but neither evaluates the developer's inference nor specifies an access design that respects both rules.
It incorrectly treats a financial review exemption as authorization to bypass an operating-system privilege restriction.

question_plan: Assess the coverage of a GBP/USD risk band under two mutually exclusive, exhaustive market regimes. question: A consumer chooses divisible quantities of lychees L and apples A to maximize U(L,A)=sqrt(LA), with a budget of 120 in each city. Per-unit prices (p_L,p_A) are (6,2) in Jinan and (2,4) in Guangzhou. Define the lychee-for-apple MRS as MU_L/MU_A. Using the chain rule to derive marginal utilities and elimination to solve the budget and optimality equations, which option gives the maximizing bundles (L,A) and their MRS values?

options.A: Jinan: (15,15), MRS=1; Guangzhou: (20,20), MRS=1. The MRS values are equal.
options.B: Jinan: (10,30), MRS=3; Guangzhou: (30,15), MRS=1/2. Jinan's MRS is higher.
options.C: Jinan: (12,24), MRS=3; Guangzhou: (20,20), MRS=1/2. Jinan's MRS is higher.
options.D: Jinan: (18,6), MRS=1/3; Guangzhou: (12,24), MRS=2. Guangzhou's MRS is higher.

explanation: The chain rule gives MU_L=A/(2sqrt(LA)) and MU_A=L/(2sqrt(LA)), so MRS=A/L. Interior utility maximization requires MU_L/MU_A=p_L/p_A. In Jinan, this gives 2A-6L=0. Subtracting it from the budget equation 6L+2A=120 yields 12L=120, hence (L,A)=(10,30). In Guangzhou, optimality gives 4A-2L=0. Subtracting it from 2L+4A=120 yields 4L=120, hence (L,A)=(30,15). These interior solutions maximize utility: along each budget, LA is a strictly concave quadratic, while boundary bundles give zero utility. The resulting MRS values are 3 and 1/2, respectively, so Jinan's is higher.

distractor_analysis.reason: It assumes symmetric utility requires equal quantities, ignoring unequal prices and the price-based optimality condition. Both bundles exhaust the budget but fail MRS=p_L/p_A.

It states the correct optimal MRS values from local price ratios but does not connect them to MRS=A/L when choosing bundles. The listed bundles are budget-feasible, but their actual MRS values are 2 and 1, not 3 and 1/2.
It equates A/L to the inverse price ratio p_A/p_L. This produces the listed budget-feasible bundles but violates the correct optimality condition and reverses the MRS comparison.

question_plan: A CPA is assessing revenue risk for a retailer selling one product. Before the current year, its uniform selling price was increased and then decreased by the same percentage, leaving the final price at 84% of the prior-year price. All current-year sales used this final price, unit sales were unchanged, and there were no other revenue drivers. Reported revenue nevertheless remained unchanged. Correctly calculate the 40% adjustments and final price of 84% of the original, but incorrectly apply an inverse price-revenue relationship despite unchanged unit sales. Predict revenue of 1/0.84 times prior-year revenue and assess the reported result against that erroneous expectation.

mathematics.necessity: The decrease applies to the increased price, so equal percentage adjustments do not cancel.

Post: My family are having issues with a trust fund set up by my father who passed away in 1998 and think we have been treated extremely unfairly for almost 20 years. This has now come to a breaking point – the trust has informed us they no longer think we (my brother and I) are beneficiaries due to an deed which was signed by Protector rather than my father and the firm are seeking legal and tax advice on the outcome of this.  In order to tell this story right I’ll section my post.   **Background:**  Relevant parties: Myself (f25), Mother (49), Brother (20), father (deceased), half-sister (no contact), half bother (no contact), my uncle who is protector (some contact but not close).  My parents were never married but had been together for 10 years. Previous to this my father was married and had two children. They divorced a few years before meeting my mother.  My father had a trust fund set up in in 1991 (before my brother and I were born but when my parents were together). My parents moved from the UK to another country were they made a life together – owning a property together, a boat and were in the process of building another property. Around 1996 my father sold his business in the UK.  The unbuilt house, the business and the boat were all assets of the trust.  My father passed away unexpectedly back in 1998 when I was around the age of five and my brother (M20) was a few months old.   **History of the Trust:**  The 1991 Deed The trust was set up in 1991 – the original trustees were UK residents. The trust was established by a deed of settlement and expressed to be a Guernsey law trust. The protector of the trust was appointed to my uncle.  The beneficiaries of the trust were declared: 1. The settlor (life tenant) 2. The spouse and any former spouse of the settlor 3. The children of the settlor.  Change of trustees 1991 The trustees retired in favour of a new trust to take over.  1997 Deed 1 – Addition of my mother: My mother was added as a beneficiary.  1997 Deed 2: This introduced different terms. To pay the income of the trust to his children and my mother in equal shares until my brother reached 25, when of which all the capital will be divided between the beneficiaries.  1999 Appointment: Additions of beneficiaries and appointment of assets A deed was prepared that added myself and my brother as beneficiaries. This was due to them finding we do not come under the definition of children for the purposes of the trust or the 1997 Appointment as our parents were unmarried. This added new terms, notably allowing the discretionary distribution of income and capital before the youngest child (my brother) turned 25.  In order to be a part of this ‘deal’, my mother put my parents shared property in the trust portfolio (this is important information – bear with me!)  Change of Trustee 2002: The trustees retired in favour of a new trust to take over. This trust remains the current trustee of the trust.  2008 Deed: Appointments of the trust fund Under the 1999 deed the trust gave my half-sister and half-brother their full amounts as they are ‘legitimate’ children.   **The Problems:**  For years my family have had battles with the trust over unfair treatment. I wont go into the details of this, it’s so lengthy and an issue itself but we have asked to leave them a number of times. We were always told its not possible for any of us (Myself, Mother, Brother, Half-sister, Half-brother). We were told we would need to wait until my brother turned 25. Over the course of the years we’ve (my immediate family – not half siblings) lost about £60,000 + combined from fees.  Back in 2015, I asked for a deposit for my first home. After a lengthy email battle over the year, they finally agreed. At some point during this it came to light that my half siblings walked away years ago (we were never made aware), and that my mother has had the ability to walk away since 2008 (again, we were never told despite continuously asking to leave). When this came to light my mother instantly asked for her funds, they agreed to start making this happen.  It didn’t happen. Instead they sent us a letter a year later stating that after investigating our Trust as something came to light which means me and my brother may not be beneficiaries after all.  In preparing my distribution for my house deposit, they reviewed the 1991 Deed concerns were found/ raised.  **Problem 1**  Basically, my dad didn’t sign the ‘Change of trustees 1991’ document despite having priority power under the terms. It was executed by my uncle – as this dates way back we aren’t sure why, perhaps my father was unavailable. But he did instruct my uncle to do so on his behalf.  The second Trustees have communication from 1994 regarding this issue – however they, and the previous trustees decided they ‘were satisfied the Settlor was not available and therefor a change of trustees executed by the protector was valid’. This was because the settlement listed three person with the power to appoint replacements ‘The settelor, the protector and the trustees’  Flash forward 20 years and a law firm now thinks that the second trustees (1991) decision was ‘wrong’ and that our current trustees should take the matter to court seeking a clear idea of the tax consequences.  The law firm advice found there are two outcomes: 1.	The 1991 retirement deed is invalid but the 2002 deed is valid.  2.	Or they are both invalid and the trust should have never moved from the UK and there will be serious tax implications. There are serious tax implications for both and the trust are currently investigating these and we are awaiting results. This investigation is costly (£10,000 so far) and the distributions are being made from our ‘accounts’ with them.   **Problem 2: Me and my brother being added post 1991 Retirement Deed.**  As the 1991 Retirement Deed is likely to be found invalid, it is also likely me and my brother are invalid as this was exercised by ‘invalid’ trustees and after my fathers death. Yet my mothers appointment is fine as this was exercised by my father while he was alive and under the terms of the original 1991 deed.  Therefor we are awaiting tax information and investigation into the 1991 deed,1997 appointment and 1999 appointment as it has bearings on 1. The tax positions 2. The validity of past distributions 3. Whether to continue with court application 4. How to respond for future requests for distributions 5. Whether the second trust have any obligation to assist.  **Where we stand**  We’re currently awaiting the tax information but the trust have said to us that they would be looking at hopefully distributing all capital to us so we can walk away from this (yeah right – I’m sure they’re going to offer that).  From our point of view we are an innocent party to this. We’re angry that: 1. It seems we will have most of the capital taken from us due to mistakes that weren’t ours. 2. That they convinced my mother to put her shared home into the trust under a now false promise. 3. They may seek the past distributions from us! 4. Our half siblings have been able to walkaway from this mess.S o many other things.  **My main questions are:** 1.	Will we be held responsible and ultimately be the ones who will have to pay for this mess? 2.	Do you think there is any room to recoup loss/ sue for this mess (fees throughout the years and the likely loss of all the capital as this has not been picked up previously (apart from the communication in 1994)? 3.	If they do come back with a resolution to this (an offer to walkaway with a sum), do you think we should consider it? I’m concerned as I feel we are still the ones who have ultimately paid the price of someone else mistake. Even in the unlikely case this was presented, for all these years we have paid so many fees, and now feed for this tax/ law firm (who we have no contact with and know nothing about!) and the fact that my mother could have walked away years ago (she has been paying fees all that time!) 4.	What type of solicitor should we be seeking advice from?  Please help! This is causing us so much distress and pain. It’s been ongoing all my life and we just want out of it now.  TL;DR  Current Trust is arguing the previous trust was invalid as a retirement deed was signed by protector rather than my father who is now deceased. This makes previous addition of me and my brother (after my dad passed) invalid and the moving of the trust to a offshore trust invalid. This could have serious tax implications for us and also removes us from the trust, making all previous distributions invalid. Basically big £££ and distress over a mistake that was not ours and was overlooked for almost 20 years. Currently being made to pay all the legal costs of this by our trust (distributions being made from the trust capital). Should we sue or seek legal action?   Also half siblings were informed they could leave early and left in 2008 with capital. Despite my mother continuously asking to leave and being told no, it has recently come to light she could of in 2008 yet they didn’t tell her and she has paid fees since then!   Please, any advice is welcome :(   FYI Despite how this story sounds my father and mother came from different backgrounds – my mother being working class. I would consider us to be working class right now so available funds are limited and all tied up in the trust. Reply with either: Yes, No

Post: Almost a year ago I contacted a housekeeping company on Craigslist. I will change names here, let's call the owners of the company Viktor and Svetlana.  Svetlana sent a cleaning lady to my apartment, we will call her Vera. Vera does a fantastic job, we like her a lot. She is very sweet and meek and deferential. She comes every other week or so as needed, we have a tiny apartment, she charges $60 and I add $10 as a tip for a total of $70, I make out a check to Vera directly every time she comes. She cleans the whole 550 sq. ft. apartment including the dishes.  Vera does not speak basically any English at all, so anything I have to say I have to communicate through Svetlana by text message. I have never met Viktor or Svetlana, but I text them to arrange cleaning or if I have some request for Vera. I have the suspicion that Svetlana may be a bit stern or mean to Vera.  This summer Vera started bringing her girls. The girls are out of school and are helping her clean. Usually I am not home when she comes, so I didn't notice at first, but I worked from home one morning and she had brought her daughter, and then another time I noticed that she has two daughters she sometimes brings. The girls are very sweet and always smiling and pleasant.   I am not certain of the age of the girls, but they are both teenagers. The older one is probably 16-17, the younger may be 14-15.  I don't know what to do.  My concerns:  - We like Vera and her girls a lot. I actually used to clean apartments myself when I was in college full-time and I can't imagine doing it as a single mother. She seems like a great mom with happy girls and we are not judging her or wanting to get her in trouble, I am confident that she is making the best choices she can for her girls. Whatever I do I do not want to make life harder for her or her girls.  - I don't know how old the girls are or if they are being compensated fairly. I can't ask Vera about this because she knows so little English she is nearly mute. I could ask Svetlana, but I don't know how much I trust Svetlana, I have never even met her.  - I have no idea how many hours a week the girls are working, I don't know how many homes Vera cleans. It seems she only brings her girls occasionally and only since the summer began, she brings the older one more often I think.  So I guess my question is, how do I know whether this arrangement is legal? Am I violating child labor laws? How do I remedy this situation in a way that is best for Vera and her girls? Reply with either: Yes, No

options.A: Send to the general queue without issue classification; this nonprofit may request a hearing before the penalty decision.
options.B: Send to the small-business/nonprofit legal-issues queue; this nonprofit may request a hearing before the penalty decision.
options.C: Small-business/nonprofit legal issues include taxes; the exercise identifies a nonprofit fined 15,000 yuan as eligible for a hearing.
options.D: Send to the small-business/nonprofit legal-issues queue; placement in this category entitles every organization to a pre-decision hearing for any fine.

My parents were never married but had been together for 10 years. Previous to this my father was married and had two children. They divorced a few years before meeting my mother.
